title: Riads Explained: Where to Stay in Morocco and Why
content:
Ask anyone who's been to Morocco where you should stay, and the answer comes back fast: a riad. For a first-timer it's one of the easiest ways to make a trip feel special — but "riad" is a word most Americans arrive not quite understanding. Here's what a riad actually is, why it's worth it, and how to pick one that fits your trip.

What is a riad?

A riad is a traditional Moroccan house or palace built inward around a central courtyard or garden, often with a fountain at its heart and rooms opening onto the open-air middle. The design turns its back on the busy street outside — thick walls, few exterior windows — and opens up internally into a calm, tiled, plant-filled sanctuary. Many have been lovingly restored and converted into small guesthouses, typically with just a handful of rooms, a rooftop terrace, and a level of personal attention closer to a bed-and-breakfast than a hotel.

The magic is the contrast: you step off a chaotic medina lane through an unremarkable door and into a hushed courtyard with a trickling fountain, intricate zellij tilework, and carved cedar. It's a genuinely Moroccan experience you can't really get anywhere else.

Why stay in a riad?

Location inside the medina

Most riads sit inside the old medina, which puts you steps from the souks, squares, and sights — exactly where you want to be, and where cars can't go anyway.

Atmosphere and hospitality

Small size means personal service: staff who help you plan days, arrange a trusted taxi, or serve mint tea when you arrive. Breakfast on a sunny rooftop terrace overlooking the medina is a standard riad pleasure.

A calm base in an intense city

Marrakech and Fez can be gloriously overwhelming. Retreating to the quiet of a riad courtyard at the end of the day is what makes the intensity sustainable.

What to know before you book

Riads are converted courtyard houses inside the medina, and booking one comes with three practical realities: they are genuinely hard to find on arrival, rooms in historic buildings vary enormously in size and light, and stairs are usually unavoidable. Good riads meet you at the nearest car-accessible point and walk you in — message the property before you arrive.

Because they're tucked into the medina maze, riads can be genuinely hard to find on arrival — good ones will arrange to meet you at a car-accessible point and walk you in, so message ahead. Rooms in historic buildings vary; some are small or dark by design, so read recent reviews and look at actual room photos. Not every riad has an elevator or easy luggage access, which matters if stairs are a concern. And while many riads take cards, some smaller ones prefer cash — check when you book.

What's usually included

Most riads include breakfast — often a generous spread of Moroccan breads, pancakes (msemen and beghrir), olives, fresh juice, and mint tea, served on the terrace or in the courtyard. Beyond that, the standout riad extra is service you won't find at a big hotel: staff will book a reliable airport transfer, arrange a trusted local guide, call ahead to a hammam, or even cook a traditional dinner on request with a little notice. Many riads also offer this home-cooked dinner as an option, which is a lovely, low-key first night when you don't want to head back out into the medina. Ask what's on offer when you book — the personal touches are the whole point.

How much do riads cost?

Riads span the full range. A simple, well-run guesthouse in the medina can be genuinely affordable, mid-range riads offer beautiful rooms and rooftop terraces for a comfortable nightly rate, and restored-palace riads climb into luxury territory with plunge pools and spa services. Because the best-reviewed small riads have only a few rooms, they book up — reserve early for peak spring and fall dates. For dollar figures across accommodation tiers, see our Morocco trip cost guide.

Riad or hotel?

You don't have to choose one for the whole trip. A common first-timer approach is to stay in riads in the atmospheric cities — Marrakech, Fez, Chefchaouen — where the experience shines, and opt for a modern hotel where it makes more sense, such as near the airport on a travel day, or in Casablanca. Out in the desert, the equivalent experience is a night in a Sahara desert camp, and in the mountains it's a kasbah or guesthouse. Matching your lodging to each place is part of the fun.

How to book a riad

Riads across Marrakech, Fez, and beyond are listed on the major booking platforms, which makes it easy to compare courtyards, rooftop terraces, locations, and recent guest reviews in one place. Filter by medina location and read the latest reviews closely — for riads more than most stays, the recent guest experience tells you what you're really getting. Once you've found one you love, message the property before arrival to arrange the medina meet-up, and you'll start your trip the right way: stepping out of the noise and into your own tiled courtyard.

Choosing where in the medina

Not all medina locations are equal, and it's worth a moment's thought. A riad deep in the heart of the old city is the most atmospheric but the hardest to reach with luggage; one nearer a main gate (a "bab") or a car-accessible edge is easier to get in and out of, especially on arrival and departure days. Light sleepers should check whether a riad sits near a mosque — the pre-dawn call to prayer carries — or above a busy lane. None of this should scare you off a medina stay; it just helps to read reviews with an eye for the practical, not only the pretty. The best riads strike a balance: immersive enough to feel special, reachable enough that day one doesn't start with a suitcase-dragging odyssey.

For where to base yourself specifically, see our guides to where to stay in Marrakech and the best riads in Marrakech for first-timers.

Where you sleep quietly decides more than comfort: it sets how far you walk, how often you take a taxi, and how much of the medina you meet on foot each day. the complete Morocco trip guide works through the base decision alongside the transport and sequencing calls it drives.

Riad FAQ

What exactly is a riad?

A traditional Moroccan house built around an interior courtyard or garden, often restored into a small, characterful guesthouse with a rooftop terrace.

Are riads worth it for first-timers?

Very much so. They put you inside the medina near the sights, offer personal service, and provide a calm retreat from busy cities — a highlight of most first trips.

Are riads expensive?

They span budgets, from simple guesthouses to lavish restored palaces, so you can find a riad experience at most price points. Book early for the best-reviewed ones.

Is it hard to find a riad in the medina?

It can be — the medina is a maze. Good riads arrange to meet you at a car-accessible point and walk you in, so message the property before you arrive.

title: Electricity, Plugs and Staying Charged in Morocco
content:
Morocco runs on European-style electricity, which means US travelers need the right adapter and, for some devices, a voltage converter — a small detail that is easy to sort before you fly and annoying to discover on arrival. Getting your charging setup right keeps phones, cameras and the rest powered through long days of sightseeing and remote desert nights. Here is exactly what Morocco uses and what to bring.

Plugs and voltage

Morocco uses the round two-pin European plug (types C and E) and runs on 220 volts at 50 hertz, the European standard, rather than the flat-pin 110-volt system of the United States. This means two things for an American traveler: your plugs will not physically fit without an adapter, and any device not rated for dual voltage could be damaged by the higher current. Both are easily solved, but both need attention before you travel.

What you need to bring

At minimum, pack a Europe-style plug adapter — ideally two or three, since you will have multiple devices and adapters are easy to misplace. Check each device's label: phones, laptops, cameras and most modern electronics are dual-voltage (marked "100-240V") and need only the adapter, while older or high-wattage items like some hair dryers and curling irons are 110V-only and require a voltage converter or risk being fried. When in doubt, read the fine print on the charger.

The dual-voltage check

The single most useful habit is to check the voltage rating printed on each charger or device before you go: if it says "100-240V" you are fine with just an adapter, which covers almost all phones, laptops and camera chargers. Only the minority of single-voltage, high-heat appliances need a converter, and often the simplest answer is to leave those at home and buy or borrow locally. This one check prevents both a dead device and a damaged one.

Staying charged on the road

Beyond the adapter, a few habits keep you powered: carry a power bank for long sightseeing days and travel legs, since you will lean on your phone for maps, photos and ride apps; and remember that remote riads, desert camps and mountain lodges may have limited or intermittent electricity. Charge everything fully whenever you have reliable power, especially before heading into the desert, where a socket may be scarce and your camera will be busy.

Charging in remote places

The desert and the mountains are where charging gets genuinely tricky: a desert camp may run on a generator for only part of the evening, and a remote mountain lodge may have limited or intermittent power, so you cannot rely on topping up whenever you like. The answer is a fully charged power bank and the discipline of charging every device to full before you leave the last town with reliable electricity. Treat power as a resource to stock up on before the empty stretches, not something always on tap.

Buying adapters and gear

Adapters are cheaper and simpler to buy at home before you travel rather than hunting for them on arrival, though you can find adapters and chargers in Moroccan cities if you forget. A universal travel adapter that also includes USB ports is a tidy single-item solution that works here and on future trips. Whatever you choose, having it sorted before departure means you are charging your phone the moment you reach your first riad, not scouring a medina for an electronics stall.

A simple charging kit

The setup that covers almost everyone: two or three European adapters, a power bank, a multi-port USB charger to power several devices from one adapter, and the right cables. This small bundle handles the cities, the riads and the desert without fuss. Add a voltage converter only if you are bringing a specific 110V appliance you cannot do without. Sorted before departure, charging becomes a non-issue for the whole trip rather than a daily scramble for a working socket.

For what else to bring, see our packing guide; for keeping connected, the eSIM and SIM guide covers data.

Morocco electricity and plugs: FAQ

What plugs does Morocco use?

Round two-pin European plugs (types C and E), at 220 volts. US flat-pin plugs won't fit without an adapter.

Do I need a voltage converter?

Only for single-voltage 110V devices like some hair dryers. Most phones, laptops and cameras are dual-voltage ("100-240V") and need just an adapter.

How do I know if a device is dual-voltage?

Check the label on the charger — "100-240V" means it's fine with an adapter alone. That covers almost all modern electronics.

How do I stay charged in the desert?

Carry a power bank and charge everything fully before heading in — remote camps and lodges may have limited or intermittent electricity.

What should my charging kit include?

Two or three European adapters, a power bank, a multi-port USB charger and your cables — plus a converter only for a specific 110V appliance.

title: Common Mistakes First-Timers Make in Morocco
content:
Most first-timer troubles in Morocco are avoidable, and they cluster into a handful of predictable mistakes: cramming too much into the itinerary, misjudging the money and the prices, and being unprepared for the desert cold or the medina intensity. Knowing them in advance is most of the cure. Here are the errors that most often trip up first-time visitors, and the simple habits that head each one off before it costs you a day or your budget.

Trying to see too much

The most common mistake is overreaching: packing five cities and the desert into a week and spending the whole trip in transit, arriving everywhere tired and seeing nothing properly. Morocco's distances are long and the roads slow, so fewer places at a humane pace beats a frantic tour. Pick two cities and one great excursion for a week, and let the trip breathe. The travelers who most enjoy Morocco are almost always the ones who did less, but did it well.

Paying the opening price

The money mistakes are predictable and expensive in aggregate: paying the first price in the souk without bargaining, taking unmetered taxis without agreeing a fare, and accepting the opening number as if it were fixed. In Morocco the first price is an invitation to negotiate, not the real one, and the traveler who knows the fair range pays close to it while the one who does not pays the tourist premium on everything. Learning to bargain and to agree fares first is the single biggest money-saver.

The closed-currency surprise

A related money error is arriving unprepared for the dirham being a closed currency you cannot buy in advance, then being caught out at the airport — or overspending and being unable to convert leftover dirham back easily at the end. Withdraw from an ATM on arrival, carry small notes, and spend down your cash before you fly. Understanding how the money works before you land removes a whole category of first-day fumbling.

Underpacking for the cold

Travelers picture Morocco as uniformly hot and pack accordingly, then freeze on a desert night or a winter evening in Marrakech, or shiver at a mountain pass. The country's temperature range is wide — hot days, cold nights, alpine mountains — so layers and genuine warm clothing for the desert and evenings are essential. This is the packing mistake people regret most, sitting cold under the desert stars they came all this way to see. Pack for the range, not the postcard.

Cultural and practical missteps

A cluster of smaller errors round out the list: dressing too revealingly for a modest culture, photographing people without asking, drinking tap water and losing a day to it, not carrying enough small cash for tips and taxis, and being naive about the friendly "helper" who materializes to guide you and then demands payment. None is serious, and each is easily avoided with a little awareness. Respect the customs, ask before you shoot, drink bottled water, and keep small notes handy.

The meta-mistake: rigidity

Finally, the subtlest error is over-planning to the point of rigidity — scheduling every hour and missing the improvised mint tea, the tempting lane, the invitation that becomes the trip's best memory. Morocco rewards a loose, curious approach within a sensible frame more than a rigid checklist. Plan the shape, protect the big pieces, and then leave slack for the country to surprise you. The travelers who let Morocco breathe are the ones who fall in love with it.

Avoiding these mistakes mostly comes down to understanding a few connected things — the money, the distances, the climate — before you go, which is exactly what the fuller planning lays out. How to sidestep the first-timer traps is worked out in the complete Morocco trip guide.

For the bargaining specifically, see our souk price guide; for the money system, the how much cash guide covers it.

First-timer mistakes in Morocco: FAQ

What's the biggest first-timer mistake?

Trying to see too much — cramming five places into a week and spending it in transit. Pick two cities and one excursion, and go at a humane pace.

How do I avoid overpaying?

Don't accept the opening price — bargain in the souk and agree taxi fares first. The first number is an invitation to negotiate, not the real one.

What do people get wrong about the weather?

They pack for heat only and freeze on desert nights or winter evenings. Pack layers and real warm clothing for the range, not the postcard.

What are the common cultural missteps?

Dressing too revealingly, photographing people without asking, drinking tap water, and trusting the "helper" who then demands payment.

What's the subtlest mistake?

Over-planning to rigidity and missing the improvised moments. Plan the shape, protect the big pieces, and leave slack for Morocco to surprise you.

title: The Sahara Desert: A First-Timer's Guide to Merzouga and Zagora
content:
For many first-time visitors, a night in the Sahara is the single most memorable part of a Morocco trip — a camel ride over golden dunes at sunset, dinner around a fire, and a sky thick with stars. It's also the leg that takes the most planning, since the desert is a long way from the cities. Here's what you need to know.

Merzouga or Zagora?

Merzouga is the right answer for most first-timers: Erg Chebbi's tall dunes are the postcard Sahara, and reaching them means a 9–10 hour drive from Marrakech, so realistically a 3-day/2-night trip. Zagora is closer and fits a 2-day/1-night trip, but its dunes are smaller and stonier. The choice is really about how many days you can give the desert.

Merzouga (Erg Chebbi)

Home to Erg Chebbi, the tall, sweeping golden dunes that look like the postcard Sahara. It's farther from Marrakech — roughly a 9–10 hour drive, so realistically a 3-day/2-night trip — but the dunes are dramatically bigger and more beautiful. For most first-timers chasing the classic desert image, Merzouga is worth the extra time.

Zagora

Closer to Marrakech and doable as a shorter 2-day/1-night trip, but the dunes are smaller and less spectacular, and the landscape is more rocky desert than towering sand. Choose Zagora if you're truly short on time; choose Merzouga if you can spare the extra day. Our detailed comparison goes deeper.

How to get there

There's no airport or train to the dunes — the Sahara is reached overland, almost always as a guided multi-day tour with a driver, or self-driven if you're adventurous. Most first-timers take the tour, because it handles the long distances and turns the drive itself into part of the trip, with spectacular stops along the way: the film-famous kasbah of Aït Benhaddou, the dramatic Todra Gorge, and the Dades and Rose valleys. See our Sahara tours from Marrakech guide for how to book.

What a desert camp night is like

The heart of the experience. In the late afternoon you'll ride a camel (or 4x4) into the dunes to your camp as the light turns gold. Camps range from simple to genuinely luxurious, but the rhythm is similar: a traditional dinner, often music around a fire, and then the main event — lying back under a sky so full of stars it's disorienting. Nights can be cold, even in summer, so layers matter. In the morning, wake for sunrise over the dunes, one of the great sights of any trip.

What to pack for the desert

A few essentials make the trip far more comfortable: layers for hot days and genuinely cold nights, a scarf (invaluable against sun and blowing sand), sunglasses and sunscreen, closed shoes plus sandals, a headlamp or flashlight, and any cash you'll need since there are no ATMs out here. Bring a small bag for the camp and leave your main luggage in the vehicle. And download offline maps and music before you go — there's little to no signal in the deep desert.

The camel ride: what it's really like

The sunset camel trek into the dunes is the iconic Sahara moment, and it's worth setting expectations. You'll ride single-file in a small caravan, led by a guide on foot, for anywhere from twenty minutes to an hour to reach camp. It's slower and more lurching than you might picture — camels rock as they stand and sit, so hold on during those moments — but the pace lets you soak in the shifting light on the dunes. If riding isn't for you (it can be uncomfortable for some backs and knees), most camps can arrange a 4x4 transfer instead, so you don't miss the camp itself. Either way, wear long pants and bring that scarf for the sand.

Simple vs. luxury desert camps

Where you sleep shapes the whole night. Basic camps offer simple tents with shared bathroom facilities and mattresses on the floor — perfectly fine for one night and cheaper. Mid-range and luxury camps have private tents with real beds, rugs, and sometimes en-suite bathrooms, plus better dinners and more comfort, for a surprisingly modest step up in price. Since this is likely your one and only desert night, many first-timers happily pay a little more for the upgrade. When you book a tour from Marrakech, check exactly which camp tier is included, as it's the biggest variable in the experience.

Is the Sahara trip suitable for everyone?

For most people, yes — but a few honest notes. The long drive and the camel ride can be tiring for very young children, older travelers, or anyone with back or mobility issues, though 4x4 transfers to camp and private tours ease this considerably. The desert is remote, with limited medical facilities and no reliable phone signal, so bring any needed medications and let someone know your plans. That said, families with kids often find the camels, dunes, and camp a huge hit, and the trip is a highlight across all ages. If a multi-day journey feels like too much, the Agafay stone desert near Marrakech offers a taste of a desert camp without the long haul, though it lacks the true Saharan dunes.

When to go

Spring (March–May) and fall (September–November) are ideal — warm days, cool but bearable nights. Summer days are brutally hot, though the dunes at sunset and night are still magical; winter nights are very cold. See our when-to-go guide to time it well. However you do it, a Sahara night tends to be the memory that outlasts all the others.

One thing worth noticing across all of this: the dune field you pick decides the length of the drive, the drive decides how many nights the desert costs you, and those nights decide what is left for the cities. The desert isn't a side trip you slot in — it is the piece the rest of the itinerary bends around. That whole chain is worked out, leg by leg, in the complete Morocco trip guide.

Sahara desert FAQ

Is Merzouga or Zagora better?

Merzouga has the tall, classic Erg Chebbi dunes but needs a 3-day trip; Zagora is closer and doable in 2 days but with smaller dunes. Most first-timers prefer Merzouga if time allows.

How many days do you need for the Sahara?

Merzouga is realistically a 3-day/2-night trip from Marrakech; Zagora can be done in 2 days/1 night.

Is a Sahara desert tour worth it?

For most first-timers it's the trip's highlight — the camel ride, camp dinner, stargazing, and sunrise over the dunes are unforgettable.

Is it cold in the Sahara at night?

Yes, often surprisingly cold even after hot days, and very cold in winter. Pack warm layers for the camp regardless of season.

title: Sahara Desert Tours from Marrakech: What to Expect
content:
The most popular way to reach the Sahara from Marrakech is an organized multi-day tour, and for good reason: it handles the long drive, the logistics, and the desert camp, turning a daunting journey into a smooth, spectacular trip. Here's exactly what to expect and how to choose a good one.

The standard route: 3 days to Merzouga

The classic tour is a 3-day/2-night loop from Marrakech to the Erg Chebbi dunes near Merzouga and back (or ending in Fez, which many travelers prefer). It's a lot of driving, but the route itself is full of highlights:

Day 1

Cross the High Atlas via the dramatic Tizi n'Tichka pass, stop at the UNESCO kasbah of Aït Benhaddou (a favorite film location), pass through Ouarzazate, and overnight in the Dades or Todra area.

Day 2

Explore the Todra Gorge, then drive on to Merzouga, arriving in time to ride camels into the dunes for sunset, dinner, and a night at a desert camp under the stars.

Day 3

Wake for sunrise over the dunes, then the long drive back to Marrakech — or onward to Fez if you booked the one-way version, which saves backtracking.

A shorter 2-day/1-night option runs to Zagora's smaller dunes if you're tight on time, but most first-timers find the extra day to Merzouga worth it. See our Sahara guide and Merzouga vs. Zagora comparison.

What's included

Most tours cover transport in a 4x4 or minivan, a driver (sometimes a separate guide), accommodation en route, the camel trek into the dunes, dinner and breakfast at the camp, and the desert camp itself. What's usually not included: lunches, drinks, tips for your driver and camp staff, and any upgrades to a luxury camp. Always confirm exactly what's covered before booking, since the cheapest tours often trim inclusions.

Group vs. private tours

Desert tours from Marrakech come in two formats: a shared vehicle with a handful of other travelers, or a private car with your own driver. The route and the camp are usually identical; what changes is the price, the pace, and who decides when you stop. Group tours suit solo travelers and couples watching the budget, private tours suit families and anyone who wants control.

Group tours

Shared vehicle with a handful of other travelers, cheaper, and sociable — many people enjoy the camaraderie of the shared journey. The pace is set by the group and the itinerary is fixed.

Private tours

Your own vehicle and driver, more expensive but flexible — you can stop when you like, adjust the pace, and choose your camp. Good for families, couples, or anyone who values comfort and control. Both deliver the same core experience; it comes down to budget and preference. Our guided vs. independent guide helps you weigh it.

Choosing a camp comfort level

Desert camps range from basic (simple tents, shared facilities) to luxury (private tents with real beds and en-suite bathrooms). Mid-range and luxury camps are surprisingly comfortable and only modestly more expensive — worth it for many first-timers, since it's likely your one desert night. Check what camp tier your tour uses.

What a desert tour costs

Prices vary widely by format and comfort level, so we don't quote a fixed figure — but the pattern is clear. Budget group tours with basic camps are very affordable and popular with younger travelers; mid-range group tours with better camps cost more but remain reasonable; and private tours with luxury camps sit at the top. What drives the price is mostly the camp tier, whether it's group or private, and the number of nights. Be wary of the very cheapest tours, which sometimes cut corners on the camp, cram in too many people, or rush the driving. Reading recent reviews and confirming exactly what's included is the best way to judge value. Our cost guide puts desert tours in the context of a whole trip's budget.

Surviving the long drive

The one honest downside of a Merzouga tour is the driving — it's a lot of hours in a vehicle, especially on the return leg. A few things make it easier: choose the one-way-to-Fez option if it fits your itinerary, so you don't repeat the drive; sit up front if you're prone to car sickness on the mountain switchbacks; bring downloaded music, podcasts, or a book since signal is patchy; and embrace the stops, which are genuinely spectacular rather than filler. The scenery — Atlas passes, kasbahs, gorges, palm oases — is a real part of the experience, not just transit. Frame it that way and the drive becomes a highlight instead of a chore.

Before and after the tour

Because tours start early and end late, plan a night in Marrakech on either side rather than trying to connect straight from a flight. Arrive a day before to rest, sort out cash, and pack a small overnight bag for the camp (you can leave your main luggage at your Marrakech riad, which most will hold for you). On return, you'll be dusty and tired, so a comfortable riad and a relaxed evening are the perfect reset. If your tour ends in Fez instead, book your onward accommodation there and have the same small-bag strategy. A little planning around the tour's edges makes the whole experience smoother.

Tips for booking

A few things that make for a better trip: book ahead in peak spring and fall seasons, when good tours fill up. Read recent reviews closely — driver quality and camp standards vary. Consider the one-way-to-Fez option to avoid a repeat of the long drive. Confirm inclusions and camp tier in writing. And build the tour into your wider plan using our 10-day itinerary, which slots the 3-day desert loop neatly into the classic route.

Choosing group or private is the easy half. The harder half is that the tour you book also fixes which city you end in, how many nights the desert takes out of your week, and what you can still fit afterwards. the complete Morocco trip guide maps how that choice ripples through the rest of the trip.

Sahara tours FAQ

How long is a Sahara tour from Marrakech?

The standard Merzouga trip is 3 days/2 nights; a shorter Zagora option runs 2 days/1 night. The Merzouga route can also end in Fez.

What's included in a desert tour?

Typically transport, driver, en-route accommodation, the camel trek, camp dinner and breakfast, and the desert camp. Lunches, drinks, and tips usually aren't — confirm before booking.

Should I book a group or private tour?

Group tours are cheaper and sociable; private tours cost more but offer flexibility and comfort. Both give the same core desert experience.

Can a Sahara tour end in Fez instead of returning to Marrakech?

Yes — many Merzouga tours offer a one-way option ending in Fez, which fits perfectly into a classic loop and avoids repeating the long drive.

title: Is the Tap Water Safe to Drink in Morocco?
content:
The practical answer on Moroccan tap water is simple: most visitors should stick to bottled or filtered water, not because the water is necessarily unsafe but because its different microbial content commonly upsets stomachs unused to it. A little care with water, ice and washed foods prevents the traveller's stomach trouble that can derail a few days. Here is what to drink, what to watch, and how to stay hydrated without a mountain of plastic.

The short answer

Stick to sealed bottled water or water you have filtered or purified yourself, particularly for the first part of your trip while your system adjusts. Tap water in cities is treated and locals drink it without issue, but visitors frequently react to the unfamiliar microbes even where the water meets local standards. The upset is usually mild and short, but it is exactly the kind of thing that costs you a sightseeing day, so caution early is worth it.

Ice, salads and the less obvious sources

Water reaches you in ways beyond the glass: ice made from tap water, raw salads and fruit rinsed in it, and toothbrushing are the common overlooked routes. At reputable hotels and tourist restaurants, ice and washed produce are generally fine; at basic street stalls, more caution helps. Peeling your own fruit, favouring cooked vegetables early on, and using bottled water to brush your teeth if you are being careful are simple habits that remove the hidden exposures.

Bottled water, done sensibly

Bottled water is cheap and universally available, so keep a supply in your room and carry one when out, checking the seal is intact when you buy. It is the easy default, and the small cost is trivial against a ruined day. Just be conscious that relying entirely on single-use bottles generates a lot of plastic over a trip, which is where a reusable solution earns its place.

Cutting the plastic

A reusable bottle with a built-in purifying filter, or purification tablets, lets you treat tap water and drink safely while cutting the plastic waste dramatically — a good investment for a longer trip or for the desert and mountains, where bottled supply thins out. For travellers who care about the environmental cost, this is the responsible middle path: safe water without the daily pile of empty bottles. Bring it from home, as such filters are hard to buy locally.

Staying hydrated in the heat

Morocco gets genuinely hot, especially in summer and the desert, so hydration is a real health matter, not just comfort — carry more water than you think you need and drink steadily through the day. Mint tea and soft drinks do not replace water in the heat. Heat and dehydration cause more trouble for visitors than the water itself, so the discipline of drinking enough safe water is the actual priority. Pair it with sun protection and shade in the fierce hours.

Water in the desert and mountains

Away from the cities, in the desert and the High Atlas, bottled water supply thins and the heat intensifies, so carry more than you expect to need and top up whenever you can — a desert camp or a mountain village may have limited stock. This is exactly where a purifying filter bottle proves its worth, letting you treat whatever water is available. Running low on water in the remote heat is a genuine risk, so err generously on how much you carry into the empty stretches.

If your stomach does turn

Should you get a mild stomach upset anyway, it usually passes in a day or two with rest, bland food and — importantly — plenty of safe fluids and rehydration salts to replace what you lose. Carry rehydration sachets and a basic anti-diarrhoeal from home for the worst of it. Persistent or severe symptoms warrant a pharmacy or doctor, both easily found in the cities, but the ordinary traveller's upset resolves on its own with sensible care.

For staying well overall, see our health and vaccinations guide; for the heat, the weather guide covers the seasons.

Morocco tap water: FAQ

Can I drink the tap water in Morocco?

Best not to — stick to bottled or filtered. It's treated and locals drink it, but visitors commonly react to the unfamiliar microbes.

What about ice and salads?

Fine at reputable hotels and restaurants; more caution at basic stalls. Peel your own fruit and favour cooked veg early on.

How do I cut the plastic waste?

A reusable bottle with a purifying filter, or purification tablets, lets you treat tap water safely. Bring it from home.

How much water do I need?

More than you think, especially in summer and the desert. Heat and dehydration trouble visitors more than the water itself.

What if I get an upset stomach?

It usually passes in a day or two with rest, bland food and safe fluids. Carry rehydration salts; see a pharmacy if it persists.

title: Bahia Palace, Saadian Tombs and the Marrakech Monuments
content:
Beyond the sensory rush of the souks and Jemaa el-Fnaa, Marrakech holds a cluster of ticketed monuments — palaces, tombs and a madrasa — that reward a calm half-day of proper sightseeing. They sit close together in the southern medina, so a single walking loop covers most of them. Here is what each one is, which are unmissable, and how to string them into one unhurried morning.

Bahia Palace

Marrakech's monuments reward slow looking rather than a quick tick, since their glory is in the detail — the carving, the tile, the play of light in a courtyard — rather than in scale. Budget more time per site than the map suggests. The Bahia Palace is the standout: a 19th-century palace of courtyards, painted cedar ceilings and intricate tilework, designed to be the greatest of its time, and it remains the most rewarding single monument in the city. Give it a proper hour to wander the rooms and gardens rather than rushing through. It is the one most first-timers remember, and the best place to see Moroccan craftsmanship at palace scale.

The Saadian Tombs

The Saadian Tombs are a 16th-century royal necropolis, sealed and forgotten for centuries before their rediscovery, and their central chamber holds some of the finest zellij tile and carved stucco in Marrakech. The site is small and can bottleneck at the famous main mausoleum, so arrive early to see it without a queue. It is compact but genuinely beautiful, and pairs naturally with the nearby Kasbah quarter.

Ben Youssef Madrasa

The Ben Youssef Madrasa, a former Islamic college and one of the largest in North Africa, is for many visitors the architectural highlight of the city: a serene central courtyard surrounded by extraordinarily detailed carving, tile and cedar. Recently restored, it is open to all visitors, unlike the mosques, and it is worth timing for early or late light when the courtyard is quietest. Do not skip it for the more famous palace.

Koutoubia Mosque

The Koutoubia Mosque anchors the skyline with its great 12th-century minaret, the model for towers in Seville and Rabat, though as a working mosque its interior is closed to non-Muslims. You admire it from outside and from the surrounding gardens, which are pleasant and free. It works best as a landmark to orient by and photograph rather than a stop in itself, and its gardens make a calm pause between the square and the palaces.

El Badi Palace, the ruin

Near the Bahia sits a very different monument: El Badi Palace, once a lavish 16th-century showpiece, now a vast, atmospheric ruin of roofless walls, sunken gardens and nesting storks. Where the Bahia shows Moroccan craftsmanship intact, El Badi shows its grand scale stripped back to bare structure, and the contrast between the two, visited back to back, is genuinely striking. Climb the terraces for a wide view over the medina rooftops.

Tickets, dress and timing

The monuments each charge a small separate entry, payable at the gate, and none requires advance booking except at peak periods. Dress modestly, as you would anywhere in Morocco, and carry small notes for the tickets and any guardian's tip. Mornings are cooler and quieter across all of them, so the earlier you start the loop, the more comfortable and crowd-free the whole cluster feels.

Stringing them together

The efficient plan is a southern-medina loop: start early at the Saadian Tombs before the crowds, walk to the nearby Bahia Palace for a longer visit, pass the Koutoubia and its gardens, and fit Ben Youssef — slightly north — either side depending on your route. Half a day covers the cluster comfortably, and doing it in the morning leaves the hot afternoon for a shaded cafe or the souks. Buy tickets at each site; they are inexpensive.

Fitting the monuments into a Marrakech visit alongside the souks, the square and a day trip is a small sequencing exercise that the wider trip repeats at every scale. How the city's pieces fit the loop is worked out in the complete Morocco trip guide.

For the rest of the city, see our Marrakech first-timer's guide; for the garden across town, the Majorelle guide covers it.

Marrakech monuments: FAQ

Which monument is the best?

The Bahia Palace — 19th-century courtyards, painted ceilings and tilework. Give it a full hour. Ben Youssef Madrasa rivals it for architecture.

Are the Saadian Tombs worth it?

Yes, for the exquisite zellij and stucco, though the site is small and bottlenecks. Arrive early.

Can I go inside the Koutoubia Mosque?

No — it's a working mosque, closed to non-Muslims. Admire the minaret from outside and enjoy the free gardens.

How long do the monuments take?

Half a day covers the southern-medina cluster comfortably. Do it in the morning and leave the afternoon for shade or the souks.

Do I need to book tickets?

No — buy inexpensive tickets at each site. Just arrive early at the smaller ones to beat the crowds.

title: Getting Online in Morocco: eSIM, SIM Cards, and Wi-Fi
content:
Getting online in Morocco is easy and cheap — far cheaper than the international day-pass your US carrier will happily sell you. The only real decision is whether you land already connected with an eSIM, or pick up a local SIM card in the arrivals hall. Both work. Which one suits you depends on your phone, your first two hours in the country, and how far off the main routes you plan to go.

eSIM or local SIM: the short answer

An eSIM is the better choice for most first-timers because it activates before you leave home, which means your phone has data the moment you switch off airplane mode in Casablanca or Marrakech. A local SIM is cheaper per gigabyte and gives you a Moroccan number, but it costs you twenty minutes in the arrivals hall and requires your passport. If your phone supports eSIM, start there.

Why arriving connected matters here

Morocco is a cash country with a closed currency, so your first act on landing is usually finding an ATM rather than a phone shop. Having data already running means you can check a map, message your riad, and confirm your airport transfer without hunting for airport Wi-Fi first. It removes the one moment in the trip where being lost and offline overlap.

Buying a local SIM: the three networks

Morocco has three mobile networks — Maroc Telecom, Orange and Inwi — and all three sell prepaid tourist packages heavy on data at prices that will feel almost implausible to an American. You can buy at the airport on arrival or at any operator shop in town, and you will need your passport, since SIMs are registered. Staff will usually set up the package for you on the spot.

Which network to pick

Maroc Telecom has the broadest rural footprint, which matters if you are heading into the Atlas or south toward the desert. Orange and Inwi are comparable in the cities and often slightly cheaper. For a standard first trip built around Marrakech, Fez, Chefchaouen and a Sahara tour, any of the three is fine — this is not a decision worth agonising over.

Where coverage actually stops

Coverage is strong 4G or 5G across the cities and along the main routes between them, and it stays usable in towns like Chefchaouen and Merzouga. It becomes patchy to nonexistent in the deep Sahara and in the remote High Atlas, which are exactly the places a first trip goes. Download offline maps for those legs before you leave the last city with signal.

What to download before the desert

Offline maps of the region, your riad and camp confirmations, and any tickets you will need on the way back are the practical list. Desert camps often have no signal at all — many advertise this as a feature — so plan on being unreachable for the night and tell anyone at home who might worry. It is one night, and it is the point.

Hotel and riad Wi-Fi

Nearly every riad, hotel and cafe in a Moroccan city offers free Wi-Fi, and in the cities it is generally fast enough for calls and photo uploads. Inside thick-walled riads, signal often reaches the courtyard and the terrace far better than it reaches individual rooms, which surprises people. Ask for the password at check-in and test it before you settle in.

What about using your US carrier?

Your American carrier will offer an international plan for Morocco, typically billed per day, and it is by far the most expensive option available to you. It buys convenience: your number keeps working and nothing changes. For a trip of a week or more the arithmetic stops making sense compared with an eSIM, and for a two-week loop it is not close. Check what your carrier charges before you leave, then compare.

The one case where it wins

If you are in Morocco for two or three nights on a business trip and your number needs to keep receiving calls and verification codes, paying your carrier is simply the least friction. That is a real scenario and it is worth naming, but it is not the first-timer's two-week loop.

Practical setup, in order

Two weeks before departure, confirm your iPhone or Android is unlocked and eSIM-capable in its settings. A day or two before, buy and install your eSIM but do not activate it yet — most plans start counting when the line connects. On landing, switch airplane mode off, let the eSIM connect, and message your accommodation. If you would rather use a local SIM, do that after clearing customs, passport in hand.

Calls, WhatsApp and staying reachable

Moroccans run on WhatsApp, and so will you within a day of landing. Riads confirm arrivals on it, drivers send their position on it, and tour operators use it in place of email. Any data plan covers this, so you rarely need actual call minutes. If you do want a Moroccan number for local calls, that is the one clear argument for a local SIM over an eSIM.

Keeping your US number alive

Most banks and airlines still send verification codes by SMS to your American number, which an eSIM does not receive unless your home line stays active. Keep your US line switched on for texts while running data on the eSIM — nearly every modern phone handles both at once. Test this at home a day before you fly, not in the arrivals hall.

Once you are connected, the rest of the arrival sequence is straightforward: cash first, then your ride into town. Our guide to the dirham covers what to do at the airport ATM, and the first-timer's overview puts the whole arrival in order.

Getting online in Morocco: FAQ

Does my American phone work in Morocco?

Yes, if it is unlocked. Moroccan networks use standard GSM bands compatible with US phones. Locked phones can only roam on your carrier's international plan.

Do I need my passport to buy a SIM card?

Yes. SIM cards in Morocco are registered to a person, so the shop or airport counter will ask for your passport before activating the line.

Is there Wi-Fi in riads?

Almost always, and it is usually free. Expect it to work best in the courtyard and on the terrace — thick riad walls block signal more than you would expect.

Will I have signal in the Sahara?

Assume not. Coverage fades well before the dunes, and most desert camps have none at all. Download offline maps and confirmations before you leave the last town.

Is a local SIM cheaper than an eSIM?

Usually yes, per gigabyte. The trade-off is that you buy it after landing, with your passport, instead of arriving already connected.

title: Merzouga vs. Zagora: Which Sahara Trip to Take
content:
Merzouga and Zagora are the two Sahara trips sold from Marrakech, and choosing between them looks like a question about scenery when it is really a question about time. Merzouga has the tall, cinematic dunes and costs you more driving; Zagora is closer and quicker with smaller, stonier dunes. Which is right depends almost entirely on how many days you can hand to the desert.

The honest difference: dunes and driving

Merzouga sits beside Erg Chebbi, the tall golden dune sea that is the postcard Sahara, and reaching it means roughly a 9 to 10 hour drive from Marrakech, so realistically a 3-day, 2-night trip. Zagora is closer, doable as a shorter 2-day, 1-night trip, but its desert is smaller and rockier rather than the sweeping sand most people picture. That trade — bigger dunes for more driving — is the whole decision.

Why most first-timers choose Merzouga

For a traveller chasing the classic desert image, Merzouga is worth the extra day, because Erg Chebbi delivers the dramatic landscape that Zagora simply does not have. The longer drive is broken by genuine highlights — the Tizi n'Tichka pass, Aït Benhaddou, the Todra Gorge — so the journey earns its length rather than merely enduring it. If the Sahara is a headline reason you came to Morocco, this is the one.

When Zagora is the right call

Zagora makes sense when time is the binding constraint rather than the scenery. If you have only a spare two days, a Zagora overnight still gives you a camel ride, a night under desert stars and a camp dinner without writing off three days of a short trip. It is the sensible answer for a week that is already full, not a lesser version of the same experience.

What both trips share

Whichever you choose, the shape is the same: a long drive out with scenic stops, a camel ride into the dunes toward sunset, a night in a camp with a communal tagine dinner and stargazing, and a sunrise before the drive back. There is no airport or train to the dunes — Errachidia exists near Merzouga but is rarely used by tourists — so both are reached overland, by tour or private driver. Most first-timers take a tour with a driver rather than self-driving.

The camp is where the money splits

Both routes offer standard and luxury camps, and this is where prices diverge more than the destination does. A standard camp is a genuine tented night with shared facilities; a luxury camp adds private bathrooms, better bedding and a quieter setting. The choice of camp changes the cost of the trip as much as the choice of Merzouga over Zagora, and it is a separate decision worth making deliberately.

From Marrakech or from Fez

Both dune fields can also be reached from Fez, and many Merzouga tours run one-way, starting in one city and ending in the other. This is genuinely useful on a classic loop, because it saves you repeating the long southern drive in reverse. A one-way Marrakech-to-Fez desert trip threads the Sahara into the middle of the itinerary instead of dangling it off one end.

Errachidia and the no-fly reality

There is a small airport at Errachidia near Merzouga, but tourists almost never use it, and there is no rail anywhere near the dunes. In practice the desert is always an overland journey, which is exactly why the driving time is the real cost of the trip and why the choice between the two dune fields is a choice about days. Plan the transport before you fall in love with a photograph of Erg Chebbi.

How the desert leg reshapes the rest

The desert is not a side excursion you slot in; it is the piece the itinerary bends around. A Merzouga trip removes three days from a week and dictates that you leave from and often return to Marrakech, while a Zagora trip frees a day for a city or the coast. Decide the desert first, then build the rest of the route around the days it leaves you.

Merzouga or Zagora, standard or luxury, from Marrakech or Fez — these choices interlock, and each one moves the others. How they fit together across a full first-timer route is worked through in the complete Morocco trip guide.

For how the tours are sold and booked, see Sahara tours from Marrakech; for the overnight itself, our desert guide covers what the night is like.

Merzouga vs Zagora: FAQ

Which has the better dunes?

Merzouga. Erg Chebbi's tall golden dunes are the classic Sahara; Zagora's are smaller and stonier.

How long does each take?

Merzouga is realistically 3 days, 2 nights because of the 9 to 10 hour drive; Zagora fits a 2-day, 1-night trip.

Is Zagora a waste of time?

No. It is the right choice when you only have two days to spare and still want a camel ride and a night in a camp.

Is there a faster way to the dunes?

Not really. There is no tourist air or rail link, so both are reached overland by tour or private driver.

Standard or luxury camp?

A separate decision. Luxury adds private bathrooms and comfort and moves the price as much as the destination choice does.

title: The Atlas Mountains: Day Trips and Longer Stays
content:
The High Atlas rises barely an hour from Marrakech, which makes it the easiest escape from the city's heat and bustle and one of the most rewarding parts of a Morocco trip. It works as a half-day outing, a full day, or a multi-day base, depending on how much time you can give it, and the choice shapes what you see — from a valley lunch to a Toubkal summit. Here is what each version offers.

What fits a day trip

A day trip from Marrakech comfortably reaches the Ourika Valley, the village of Imlil at the foot of Toubkal, or the Berber villages and waterfalls of the foothills, all within easy driving distance. These outings trade the desert's drama for green valleys, running water and mountain air, and they are the perfect antidote to a few hot days in the medina. A driver or organised tour handles the winding roads and leaves you free to walk and look.

Ourika and Imlil

The Ourika Valley is the classic easy day trip — a river, waterfalls, and roadside cafes an hour from the city — while Imlil is the gateway village for Toubkal and a lovely destination in its own right for a valley walk and lunch. Either gives you a genuine taste of the mountains without an overnight, and both pair naturally with a Marrakech-based trip that wants one day of altitude and green.

What needs longer

Serious walking and the real high country need more than a day: trekking Mount Toubkal, North Africa's highest peak, is typically a two-day guided climb from Imlil, and multi-day village-to-village treks reward those who want to go deeper. Staying a night or two in a mountain guesthouse or a valley kasbah turns the Atlas from a glimpse into an experience, and the pace up here is the point rather than a limitation.

How to reach it

The mountains are reached by road from Marrakech, and most first-timers go with a driver or on an organised tour rather than self-driving the steep, winding routes. A hired car with a driver is flexible and affordable for a day, while trekking trips include transfers to the trailhead. The roads are scenic but demanding, which is exactly why handing the wheel to someone who knows them is the common and sensible choice.

What to wear and bring

The mountains run cooler than Marrakech year-round and cold at altitude, so a warm layer belongs in the daypack even on a summer day trip, along with sturdy shoes for uneven ground, sun protection, and water. Weather shifts quickly at height, and a valley that is warm at midday chills fast in shade or late afternoon. Packing for a range of conditions turns a day trip from uncomfortable into easy.

Combining the Atlas with the desert

Many Sahara tours from Marrakech cross the High Atlas on the way south, over the dramatic Tizi n'Tichka pass, so a desert trip already gives you a taste of the mountains in transit. If the Atlas is a headline reason you came, though, a dedicated day or overnight rewards it far better than the drive-through glimpse. Deciding which you want shapes how you build the southern part of the trip.

When to go

Timing matters more in the mountains than in the cities: spring and autumn are ideal, summer offers cool relief from the lowland heat, and winter brings snow to the high passes and peaks, with Toubkal becoming a technical winter climb. A valley day trip works most of the year; a serious trek should be matched to the season and, for the high routes in winter, to proper mountain conditions.

Fitting the Atlas into a trip — a day from Marrakech, or a longer base — is a sequencing choice that trades against the desert and the cities for your limited days. How those pieces balance is worked out in the complete Morocco trip guide.

For the base you'd day-trip from, see our Marrakech guide; for reaching the mountains, the car and driver guide covers the drive.

Atlas Mountains: FAQ

Can I visit the Atlas on a day trip?

Yes — the Ourika Valley, Imlil, and foothill villages are all within an hour or so of Marrakech, ideal for a day of green and mountain air.

How do I climb Toubkal?

Typically a two-day guided climb from Imlil. It's North Africa's highest peak and a winter climb becomes technical.

Should I self-drive?

Most don't. The roads are steep and winding, so a driver or organised tour is the common, sensible choice.

When's the best time?

Spring and autumn are ideal, summer offers cool relief, and winter brings snow to the peaks and passes.

Is a night in the mountains worth it?

Yes, if you can spare it — a valley kasbah or guesthouse turns a glimpse into a real experience.

title: What to Eat in Morocco: The Essential Dishes
content:
Moroccan food is one of the great pleasures of a trip, and knowing the essential dishes before you arrive turns a bewildering menu into a plan. The staples belong to a broader North African and Mediterranean culinary tradition, rendered in a distinctly Moroccan style, and a first-timer can eat superbly for very little by knowing what to seek out. Here are the dishes worth prioritising, what each one is, and how to order them well.

Tagine: the everyday centrepiece

The tagine — a slow-cooked stew named for the conical earthenware pot it is made in — is the dish you will eat most, and its Moroccan versions are superb: chicken with preserved lemon and olives, lamb with prunes and almonds, or a vegetable tagine rich with spices. Every region and cook has their own, so it rewards repeat ordering. Served with bread to scoop rather than cutlery, it is comforting, cheap and endlessly varied.

Couscous: the Friday dish

Couscous — steamed semolina grains topped with vegetables and meat — is a North African staple traditionally eaten on Fridays, and a proper Moroccan couscous, mounded high with seven vegetables and tender meat, is a feast. Because the authentic version is a Friday ritual, that is the best day to seek it out, when homes and restaurants make it fresh. It is generous, sociable food, meant to be shared from a communal dish.

Pastilla and the savoury-sweet tradition

Pastilla is the showpiece: a flaky pie, traditionally of pigeon (now often chicken), dusted with cinnamon and sugar over a savoury spiced filling — the savoury-sweet combination that runs through the region's festive cooking. It is richer and more elaborate than everyday food, so it is worth ordering once at a good restaurant to understand this side of the cuisine. It captures a whole tradition of celebration food in a single dish.

Street food and snacks

The street food is where the everyday flavour lives: grilled skewers (brochettes), bowls of spiced snails from a cart, fried sardines on the coast, sfenj (the North African fried dough rings) at breakfast, and fresh bread from neighbourhood ovens. Jemaa el-Fnaa in Marrakech turns this into a nightly food theatre. Eating where locals queue, and confirming prices at tourist-heavy stalls, gets you the best of it cheaply and safely.

Bread, salads and the supporting cast

Every meal arrives with khobz, the round flatbread used as an edible utensil, and often a spread of cooked and raw Moroccan salads — zaalouk of smoky aubergine, taktouka of peppers and tomato, and others — that are a highlight in their own right. Harira, the hearty soup of tomatoes, lentils and chickpeas, is the traditional way to break the fast in Ramadan and a satisfying meal any time. These sides are half the pleasure of eating here.

Regional specialities worth chasing

Beyond the national staples, the regions reward a curious eater: the coast at Essaouira and along the Atlantic serves superb grilled fish and seafood straight off the boats; the south and the desert lean on hearty tagines and dates; and Fez is known for refined, elaborate cooking including its own take on pastilla. Ordering the local speciality wherever you are — asking what the region or town is known for — turns a week of meals into a tour of the country's genuine culinary variety.

Sweets and pastries

The sweet tradition deserves its own attention: honey-soaked pastries, almond-stuffed cookies, sesame and nut confections, and dates are served with tea and at celebrations, and they are part of a wider regional culture of festive sweets. A plate of assorted pastries with mint tea is the classic way to end a meal or fill an afternoon pause. They are intensely sweet by design, so a little goes a long way, but sampling them is part of eating your way through the country.

How to eat well as a first-timer

The strategy that works: eat tagine and salads freely at casual places, seek out couscous on a Friday, order pastilla once at a good restaurant, graze the street food where locals do, and finish with mint tea and pastries. Ask what is fresh and regional rather than ordering the same thing everywhere. Eat this way and Morocco is one of the world's great affordable food destinations, with genuine variety across its regions and cities.

Food is woven into the texture of the whole trip — the mint tea offered in every shop, the meals that punctuate the sightseeing — and how it fits the days and the budget is worked out in the complete Morocco trip guide.

For a hands-on introduction, see our cooking classes guide; for eating without meat, the vegetarian and vegan guide covers it.

What to eat in Morocco: FAQ

What's the one dish I have to try?

Tagine — the slow-cooked stew you'll eat most, in endless regional variations. Chicken with preserved lemon or lamb with prunes are classics.

When can I get couscous?

Traditionally Fridays, when it's made fresh as the week's communal dish. Seek it out that day for the authentic version.

What is pastilla?

A flaky savoury-sweet pie, traditionally pigeon, dusted with cinnamon and sugar. Order it once at a good restaurant — it's festive, elaborate food.

Is the street food safe?

Largely yes, where locals queue. Eat at busy stalls, confirm prices at tourist spots, and go where turnover is high.

What comes with every meal?

Khobz bread as an edible utensil, and often a spread of cooked and raw salads — a highlight in their own right.

title: Vegetarian and Vegan in Morocco: How to Eat Well
content:
Morocco is more accommodating to vegetarians than many travellers fear, thanks to a cuisine rich in vegetables, legumes and bread, but it holds a few traps — hidden meat stock, the assumption that chicken is not "meat" — and it is genuinely harder for strict vegans. Knowing which dishes work, what to ask, and the phrases that head off misunderstandings lets plant-based travellers eat very well. Here is how to navigate it.

Why it's easier than you'd think

Moroccan cooking leans heavily on vegetables, pulses and grains, so much of the supporting table is already plant-based: the cooked and raw salads, bread, olives, and vegetable tagines are everywhere and excellent. A vegetarian can assemble satisfying meals from these without special requests in most places. The abundance of vegetable dishes means you are rarely stuck with a plain plate, which is the fate vegetarians often expect in a meat-forward country.

The dishes that work

The reliable vegetarian options are the vegetable tagine, couscous with vegetables (confirm the broth), the array of salads, lentil and chickpea dishes, and bread with dips like zaalouk. Harira soup is often but not always vegetarian, since it can be made with or without meat stock, so it is worth checking. Between the tagines, the salads and the legume dishes, a vegetarian has real variety rather than a single fallback.

The hidden-stock trap

The main pitfall is stock: a "vegetable" couscous or soup may be built on a meat broth, since that is the default in many kitchens, so asking specifically whether the broth is meat-free matters. Similarly, be explicit that you eat no meat at all, because in some places chicken or even meat stock may not register as "meat" in the way you intend. Clear, specific questions prevent the well-meaning misunderstanding that puts stock in your "vegetarian" dish.

Vegan is harder

Strict veganism is more challenging, because bread may contain butter, tagines may use ghee or a meat base, and pastries are rich with butter and eggs, so the plant-based-by-default dishes need more careful checking. The salads, plain vegetable dishes, fruit, olives and bread (confirm no butter) remain safe staples. Vegans travel best by learning to ask precise questions and by anchoring meals on the clearly plant-based dishes rather than assuming a vegetable name guarantees vegan content.

The phrases and habits that help

Learning a few key phrases pays off: how to say you eat no meat, no chicken, and (for vegans) no butter or eggs, ideally in French or with a card in Arabic. Choosing restaurants that see enough travellers to understand dietary requests, and cooking classes or riads that cater to them, smooths the trip further. Stating your needs clearly and early, rather than mid-meal, is the single most effective habit for eating well without animal products here.

Where plant-based eating is easiest

The tourist-facing restaurants of Marrakech, Fez and the other main cities increasingly understand vegetarian and vegan requests and often flag suitable dishes on the menu, so eating out in the cities is the easy part. It gets trickier in smaller towns, on the road, and at basic local eateries, where the concept may be less familiar and the safe options fewer. Planning your more careful meals around the cities, and carrying snacks for the gaps, smooths the rural and travel days.

Cooking classes and riads help

Booking a cooking class that caters to your diet, or a riad that does, is a reliable way to eat well and learn the plant-based side of the cuisine at the same time, since Moroccan cooking has so many naturally vegetable-forward dishes to teach. Mentioning your requirements when you book lets them plan the market trip and menu around them. It is one of the more enjoyable ways to guarantee a few excellent meals that fit your needs.

Eating well, plainly

The bottom line: vegetarians can eat abundantly and easily with a little checking on stock, while vegans should plan more, ask precisely, and lean on the naturally plant-based dishes. Neither needs to go hungry — Moroccan cuisine's vegetable wealth is genuinely on your side — but both benefit from clear communication. Do that, and the country's food is a pleasure rather than a puzzle, whatever you do or do not eat.

Dietary needs are one thread in how you eat across the trip, alongside the markets, the street food and the cooking classes, and how food fits the days is worked out in the complete Morocco trip guide.

For the dishes in general, see our what to eat guide; for learning to cook them, the cooking classes guide covers it.

Vegetarian and vegan in Morocco: FAQ

Is Morocco good for vegetarians?

Easier than expected — vegetable tagines, couscous, salads, and legume dishes are everywhere. The main trap is hidden meat stock.

What should I watch for?

Meat stock in "vegetable" couscous or soup, and the assumption that chicken isn't "meat." Ask specifically and state you eat no meat at all.

Is it hard to be vegan?

Harder — bread may have butter, tagines may use ghee or meat base, pastries have butter and eggs. Lean on salads, plain veg, fruit and checked bread.

What dishes are reliably vegetarian?

Vegetable tagine, veg couscous (check broth), the salads, lentil and chickpea dishes, bread with dips. Harira soup varies — ask.

What phrases should I learn?

No meat, no chicken, and for vegans no butter or eggs — in French or on an Arabic card. State needs clearly and early.

title: Moroccan Food: 15 Dishes Every First-Timer Should Try
content:
Moroccan cuisine is one of the great pleasures of a trip here — fragrant, generous, and built on centuries of Berber, Arab, and Mediterranean influence. For a first-timer, knowing what to order turns every meal into an adventure. Here are the essential dishes and drinks to seek out.

The essential main dishes

Tagine

The dish you'll eat most — a slow-cooked stew named for the conical clay pot it's made in. Classic versions include chicken with preserved lemon and olives, lamb with prunes and almonds, and kefta (meatball) with egg. Endlessly varied and always comforting.

Couscous

Traditionally the Friday family meal — fluffy steamed semolina topped with vegetables and meat. If you see couscous offered on a Friday, that's the day to order it.

Pastilla (bastilla)

A showstopper, especially in Fez — a sweet-and-savory pie of poultry (traditionally pigeon), almonds, and spices in flaky pastry, dusted with cinnamon and sugar. Unexpected and delicious.

Harira

A hearty tomato, lentil, and chickpea soup, especially popular for breaking the fast during Ramadan but served year-round. Comforting and cheap.

Mechoui

Slow-roasted whole lamb, tender and simple, often found at special stalls and celebrations.

Street food and snacks

Some of the best eating is on the street. Look for msemen (flaky square griddle pancakes) and beghrir (spongy "thousand-hole" pancakes) at breakfast; sfenj (North African doughnuts); grilled skewers (brochettes); bowls of snails in spiced broth at the markets; and freshly squeezed orange juice from the stalls in Jemaa el-Fnaa. In coastal Essaouira, don't miss the port's grilled fish. A street food guide helps you choose safely — busy stalls with high turnover are the ones to trust.

What to drink

Mint tea

The national drink and a symbol of hospitality — green tea brewed strong with fresh mint and plenty of sugar, poured theatrically from height. You'll be offered it constantly; accepting is part of the culture.

Coffee and juices

Coffee is popular (often as nous-nous, half coffee half milk), and fresh fruit juices are everywhere and cheap. On the question of alcohol — it's available for tourists in licensed hotels, restaurants, and bars, though not consumed openly in public; our alcohol guide explains.

Breakfast, the underrated meal

Moroccan breakfast deserves its own mention because it's a delight and often included at riads. Expect a spread rather than a single plate: an assortment of breads (including msemen and beghrir pancakes) served with honey, olive oil, amlou (an addictive almond-argan-honey spread), jam, and soft cheese, alongside olives, eggs, fresh orange juice, and of course mint tea or coffee. It's a leisurely, generous start to the day and one of the quiet pleasures of staying in a riad. If your accommodation offers it, lingering over a rooftop breakfast in the morning light is a lovely way to begin before the medina wakes up fully.

The Moroccan meal and hospitality

Eating in Morocco is as much about the ritual as the food. Meals often begin with an array of small salads and warm bread, build to a shared central dish everyone eats from — traditionally with the right hand and a piece of bread as your utensil — and end with fruit, sweets, and tea. Hospitality is central: if you're invited into a home, expect to be fed generously and repeatedly, and refusing outright can cause offense, so pace yourself and accept graciously. Bread (khobz) is sacred and appears at every meal, used to scoop and mop. Understanding this rhythm helps you relax into meals rather than rush them, which is exactly how they're meant to be enjoyed.

Sweets and pastries

Save room for Moroccan sweets: chebakia (sesame, honey-soaked flower-shaped cookies), briouat (sweet stuffed pastries), gazelle horns (kaab el ghazal, almond-filled crescents), and endless date and nut confections, all lovely with mint tea. They're a fixture of hospitality and celebration.

Tips for eating well

A few pointers: eat where locals eat for the best and cheapest food; use your right hand for eating, especially from shared dishes; and consider a cooking class or food tour early in your trip to learn the dishes and shop the souk with a guide — one of the most rewarding activities in the country. Stick to bottled water, and give your stomach a day to adjust before going all-in on street food. Above all, come hungry and curious — Moroccan food is a highlight in its own right.

A note on food safety

Most visitors eat wonderfully in Morocco without any trouble, but a little care prevents the common traveler's stomach. Drink bottled or filtered water and avoid ice from uncertain sources, especially early in your trip. Choose busy stalls and restaurants with high turnover, where food is fresh and constantly cooking. Fruit you can peel yourself is a safe bet. Give your system a day or two to adjust before diving into the most adventurous street food. And carry a basic stomach remedy just in case. None of this should stop you from eating widely — the food is a highlight — it just tilts the odds firmly in your favor so you can enjoy every tagine and pastry. When in doubt, follow the crowds — a stall packed with locals is both a sign of great food and of high, safe turnover. It's the single most reliable rule of thumb for eating well and safely anywhere in Morocco, from a Marrakech square to a roadside stop on the way to the desert.

Moroccan food FAQ

What is the most famous Moroccan dish?

Tagine — a slow-cooked stew named for its conical clay pot — is the most iconic, followed closely by couscous and, in Fez, pastilla.

Is Moroccan food spicy?

Not usually hot-spicy — it's aromatic and warmly spiced (cumin, cinnamon, saffron, ginger) rather than fiery. The condiment harissa adds heat if you want it.

What should vegetarians eat in Morocco?

Vegetable tagines, couscous, lentil and chickpea dishes, salads, and bread are widely available, though always confirm dishes are meat-free, as some use meat broth.

Is street food safe in Morocco?

Generally yes at busy stalls with high turnover. Stick to bottled water, give your stomach a day to adjust, and choose popular spots over quiet ones.

title: Morocco Weather by Region and Season
content:
Morocco is not one climate but several, and a trip that crosses the coast, the imperial cities, the desert and the mountains can span a startling range of conditions in a single week. Understanding how each region behaves by season is the key to timing your trip and — just as importantly — packing for it, since you may need shorts and a warm jacket in the same suitcase. Here is what to expect where, and when.

The imperial cities: hot summers, mild winters

Marrakech, Fez and Meknes inland share a broadly similar pattern: very hot, dry summers, pleasant springs and autumns, and mild but chilly winters with cold nights. These cities are most comfortable in spring and autumn, uncomfortable at midday in high summer, and cool enough in winter to need a jacket after dark. For most first-timers touring the cities, the shoulder seasons are the clear choice, avoiding both the summer furnace and the winter chill.

The coast: milder and steadier

The Atlantic coast — Essaouira, Casablanca, Agadir — is markedly milder and more temperate than the interior, cooled by ocean breezes that take the edge off summer heat and keep winters gentle. Essaouira in particular is famously windy, wonderful for a summer escape from the inland heat but breezy year-round. If summer is your only option, building in coastal time is a smart way to stay comfortable while the interior bakes.

The Sahara: extremes at both ends

The desert is a study in extremes: scorching by day and cold by night year-round, dangerously hot in summer, and genuinely freezing on winter nights despite warm daytime sun. Spring and autumn are the sweet spots for a desert trip, with warm days and merely cool nights. Whenever you go, the day-to-night swing is large, so a desert excursion always demands both sun protection and warm layers for after dark — even in the warmer months.

The Atlas Mountains: alpine rules

The High Atlas follows mountain logic: cooler than the lowlands year-round, warm and green in spring and summer at accessible altitudes, and snow-covered in winter, when high passes can close. Trekkers favour spring through autumn; winter turns the peaks alpine and cold. If your trip includes mountain hiking or a pass en route to the desert, the season dictates what is possible, and winter snow can reroute or block high tracks entirely.

Packing for a multi-region trip

Because a single itinerary can cross these zones, the packing rule is layers: light, breathable clothing for the hot cities and desert days, warm layers and a jacket for desert and mountain nights and winter evenings, sun protection everywhere, and modest coverage for cultural respect. A trip combining Marrakech, the Sahara and the Atlas in shoulder season genuinely needs both a sun hat and a fleece. Packing for the range, not the average, is how you stay comfortable throughout.

Rain and when it falls

Morocco is dry for much of the year, but the wetter months run through late autumn to early spring, when the north and the coast see most of their rain and the mountains their snow — occasionally enough to disrupt driving routes and mountain passes in winter. Summer is reliably dry almost everywhere. If you travel in winter, build a little flexibility into mountain and desert legs in case weather reroutes them, and pack something waterproof for the coast and the north.

Timing the whole trip

The season that serves the most regions at once is spring or autumn, comfortable across cities, coast, desert and accessible mountains alike, which is why they are the classic windows. Summer pushes you toward the coast and away from midday and the desert; winter opens mild city sightseeing but complicates the mountains and chills the desert nights. Choosing your dates around the regions you most want to see is the way to get the weather working for you rather than against.

Weather ties directly to routing — which regions you can comfortably combine, and when — so it shapes the whole shape of a trip. How climate and itinerary fit together is worked out in the complete Morocco trip guide.

For the city specifically, see our best time for Marrakech guide; for what to bring, the packing guide covers the layers.

Morocco weather: FAQ

What's the best overall season?

Spring and autumn — comfortable across cities, coast, desert and accessible mountains at once. That's why they're the classic windows.

How different are the regions?

Very. Hot-summer inland cities, mild Atlantic coast, extreme-swing desert, and alpine mountains — sometimes all in one week's itinerary.

Is the desert cold at night?

Yes, year-round — and freezing on winter nights despite warm days. Always pack warm layers for a desert trip, whatever the season.

When can I hike the Atlas?

Spring through autumn. Winter brings snow and can close high passes, turning the mountains alpine and cold.

How do I pack for such range?

In layers — breathable clothes for hot days, a jacket and fleece for desert and mountain nights, sun protection everywhere, modest coverage.

title: Street Food in Morocco: What's Safe and What to Skip
content:
Street food is one of the great pleasures of a Morocco trip, and eating it well comes down to a few reliable rules rather than avoiding it out of caution. The best food is often the cheapest, cooked in front of you at a busy stall, and the traveller who eats only in hotels misses a large part of the country. The trick is reading which stalls to trust, and one firm habit about water.

The one rule that covers most of it

Eat where the locals are eating, at stalls with a steady crowd and high turnover, because busy means fresh and fresh means safe. A stall working through its ingredients quickly is cooking to order rather than letting food sit, which is the single biggest factor in eating street food without trouble. An empty stall with food standing under a lamp is the one to walk past, however convenient.

Watch it cooked

Prefer food cooked or grilled to order in front of you, hot and fresh off the heat, over anything pre-prepared and held warm. Heat is the reliable safeguard, and seeing your food hit the grill removes most of the guesswork. This applies from the Jemaa el-Fnaa food stalls to a roadside grill on a desert drive.

The water rule

Tap water in Moroccan cities is officially chlorinated but commonly causes stomach upset for visitors, so stick to bottled or filtered water throughout, and avoid ice from sources you cannot vouch for. Use bottled water even for brushing teeth if your stomach is sensitive. This one habit prevents the most common traveller illness far more reliably than avoiding any particular food does.

Jemaa el-Fnaa after dark

The great set piece of Moroccan street food is Marrakech's Jemaa el-Fnaa at dusk, when dozens of numbered food stalls assemble in the square and fill with smoke and crowds.
