It is touristy and wonderful at once, and the same rules apply: pick a stall busy with locals as well as visitors, watch the food cooked, and agree what you are ordering. Some stalls pad the bill with unordered extras, so confirm prices as plates arrive.

The unordered-extras habit

At the busiest tourist stalls, small dishes of bread, olives or salad may land on your table unbidden and appear on the bill. This is not sinister and it is easily managed: if you do not want them, wave them away as they arrive rather than letting them accumulate. A quick check of the bill against what you actually ordered settles the rest.

Safe bets to seek out

Some street foods are both delicious and low-risk by their nature: freshly grilled brochettes and kefta, bowls of harira soup ladled hot from a pot, msemen and other griddle breads cooked to order, freshly fried sfenj doughnuts, and fruit you peel yourself. Freshly squeezed orange juice from a busy stall is a classic, though ask for it without ice if you are being careful. These reward the adventurous eater and rarely cause trouble.

What to be cautious with

A few things warrant more care: pre-cut fruit and salads washed in tap water, anything lukewarm that should be hot, raw or lightly cooked shellfish away from the coast, and dishes that have clearly been sitting out. The famous snail soup and the sheep's-head stalls of Jemaa el-Fnaa are authentic experiences, not dangers in themselves, but they are best approached at busy, high-turnover stands.

Ease into it

If your stomach is cautious, give it a day or two to adjust before diving into the most adventurous stalls, and carry basic remedies just in case. A mild upset is common and usually brief; it is rarely the food poisoning travellers fear, and it should not stop you eating the country properly. Most people find their footing quickly.

Eating well in Morocco is less about avoiding street food than about reading a stall the way you learn to read a price or a guide — the same attentiveness, pointed at the grill. Our guide to Moroccan dishes covers what to order, and the safety guide puts food in the wider picture.

Morocco street food: FAQ

Is street food in Morocco safe?

Largely yes, if you eat where locals eat, at busy stalls with high turnover, and choose food cooked hot to order in front of you.

Can I drink the tap water?

Stick to bottled or filtered water. City tap water is chlorinated but commonly upsets visitors' stomachs. Avoid unknown ice.

What are the safest things to eat?

Freshly grilled brochettes and kefta, hot harira soup, griddle breads cooked to order, sfenj, and fruit you peel yourself.

What should I be careful with?

Pre-cut fruit and salads, anything lukewarm, raw shellfish away from the coast, and food that has been sitting out.

Will I get sick?

A mild upset is common and brief, usually from water rather than food. Ease in over a day or two and carry basic remedies.

title: What to Pack for Morocco
content:
Packing for Morocco trips people up because a single trip spans genuinely different conditions: hot city days, cold desert nights, modest-dress expectations, and miles of walking on uneven medina ground. Pack for only the heat and the desert night ambushes you; pack heavy and the medina stairs punish you. The goal is a light bag that covers a wide range, and that comes down to a handful of deliberate choices.

Dress modestly, and layer for it

Morocco is a Muslim country where covered shoulders and knees are the respectful norm, so the core wardrobe is loose, lightweight clothing that covers without overheating. Breathable trousers, long skirts and tops with sleeves handle both the modesty expectation and the sun. A light scarf is the single most useful item, working for sun, mosque surroundings, cool evenings and dusty desert roads all at once.

Why loose beats light

In the heat, loose covered clothing is genuinely more comfortable than shorts and a tank top, because it keeps the sun off your skin while letting air move. It also removes the constant low-level attention that more revealing clothing draws. This is the rare case where the respectful choice and the comfortable choice are the same choice.

Warm layers for the desert and mountains

The Sahara and the High Atlas get genuinely cold after dark, even when the cities are hot, and this catches out travellers who packed only for a warm holiday. A warm fleece or jacket, plus something long-sleeved to sleep in at a desert camp, is essential rather than optional. Nights under the dunes drop far more than the daytime heat suggests.

Shoes for uneven ground

You will walk a great deal on uneven, sometimes slippery medina stones and packed earth, so closed, comfortable, broken-in walking shoes matter more than any style consideration. Sandals are fine for downtime but poor for a full day in the souks. If a desert trip involves any walking on dunes, know that footwear fills with sand instantly — many people simply go barefoot for that part.

Sun, water and small practicalities

Strong sun means a hat, sunglasses and high-factor sunscreen earn their space year-round. A refillable water bottle is useful, though stick to bottled or filtered water to drink. Pack any medications you rely on, since specific brands can be hard to find, and bring a small supply of hand sanitiser and tissues — public facilities do not always provide either.

Power and connectivity

Morocco uses European-style two-pin plugs, so bring the right adapter, and a power bank is worth carrying for long days out and desert nights with no sockets. Download offline maps before rural legs where signal disappears. These are small items that prevent specific, predictable annoyances rather than general ones.

A small daypack for the cities

A light daypack earns its place for city days and the desert, carrying water, a scarf, sunscreen, a power bank and whatever you buy along the way. Worn on the front in dense souk crowds, it also sidesteps the pickpocketing that thrives on distraction. Choose one that closes properly rather than an open tote, and it doubles as your desert-camp overnight bag when the main luggage stays behind.

Packing for the desert overnight

Most desert trips let you leave the main bag at a Marrakech riad or the camp's base kasbah and take only an overnight bag into the dunes. Pack that small bag with the warm layer, something to sleep in, a toothbrush, water and a charged power bank, since camps often have no power. Travelling into the dunes light, with the bulk left behind, is far more comfortable than dragging a full case across sand.

What you don't need to bring

Skip the dirham — you cannot buy it before you arrive anyway — and skip overpacking clothes, since laundry is cheap and easy and a scarf or two restyles an outfit. Leave expensive jewellery and anything you would hate to lose at home. Morocco is a place to travel light through, and a bag you can carry up a riad staircase yourself is worth more than any single item you left behind.

Most of this packing list traces back to the country's real shape — the heat-and-cold spread, the modesty norm, the walking, the closed currency you cannot pre-buy. Our best-time-to-visit guide covers how the seasons change the list, and the first-timer's overview ties the whole trip together.

Packing for Morocco: FAQ

Do I need to dress conservatively?

Covered shoulders and knees are the respectful norm. Loose, lightweight clothing handles both modesty and the heat, and draws less attention.

Is it really cold in the desert?

Yes, after dark, even when cities are hot. Bring a warm layer and something long-sleeved to sleep in at a desert camp.

What shoes should I bring?

Closed, comfortable, broken-in walking shoes for the uneven medina ground. Sandals are fine only for downtime.

What's the most useful single item?

A light scarf — it works for sun, cool evenings, dusty roads and covering up near mosques.

What should I not pack?

Dirham (you can't buy it in advance), too many clothes (laundry is cheap), and anything valuable you'd hate to lose.

title: Where to Stay in Marrakech: Neighborhoods Compared
content:
Marrakech gives you four genuinely different places to sleep, and the choice does more work than any other booking on a first trip. It sets how much of the city you reach on foot, how often you take a taxi, how quiet your nights are, and how the medina feels — as somewhere you live for a few days, or somewhere you visit. Here is what each area actually gives you.

The medina: inside the walls

The medina is where most first-timers should stay, because it puts Jemaa el-Fnaa, the souks, the Bahia Palace and the Saadian Tombs within walking distance of the front door. You will stay in a riad rather than a hotel, cars cannot reach most addresses, and arrival means meeting someone at a car-accessible point and walking in. That last detail is the whole trade-off in miniature.

What you gain and what you give up

You gain immersion and a short walk to almost everything worth seeing, and you give up convenience: luggage over uneven lanes, noise that starts early, and the genuine possibility of getting lost on your first night. For three or four days, most people find the exchange overwhelmingly worth it.

Gueliz: the new town

Gueliz is Marrakech's modern quarter, laid out in ordinary streets with international hotels, cafes with chairs on the pavement, and traffic that behaves like traffic. It suits travellers who want a familiar hotel, easy taxi access and a quiet night, and it sits roughly a short petit-taxi ride from the medina walls. Many returning visitors prefer it precisely because it feels like a working city.

The taxi arithmetic

Staying in Gueliz means the medina becomes a destination you travel to, usually twice a day. Each hop is inexpensive on its own, but it adds a small tax of time and negotiation to every outing. Over four days that is a different trip, not a worse one.

Hivernage: quiet and upscale

Hivernage sits between Gueliz and the medina, built around large hotels, gardens and wide avenues, and it is the calmest central option. It works well for travellers who want space, a pool and a peaceful night while staying close enough for easy access to the old city. It is not where you meet Marrakech, but it is a comfortable base from which to visit it.

Where the airport fits

Marrakech Menara sits about fifteen minutes from the medina, which is close enough that no area is meaningfully better or worse for the airport run. Gueliz and Hivernage are marginally quicker and simpler because a car reaches the door; a medina riad means the last stretch is on foot with your bags. It is worth a thought only for very early departures.

Splitting the stay

A pattern that works well on longer trips is two or three nights in a medina riad followed by a night somewhere with a pool before flying out or heading to the coast. You get the immersion while it is novel and the comfort when you are tired, and the transfer between the two costs one short taxi ride.

Palmeraie: resort territory

The Palmeraie is a palm grove outside the centre with resort-style hotels, big pools and quiet gardens, and it is a fifteen-to-twenty-minute drive from anything in town. Choose it deliberately, for a stay built around the hotel with occasional excursions into the city. Choosing it by accident, expecting to wander into the souks after dinner, is the classic first-timer mistake.

What the map does not show

Two riads a hundred metres apart on a map can feel entirely different to reach, because medina distance is measured in turns rather than metres. One sits three lanes off a main artery with a clear line to the square; the other requires six turns through a residential quarter that empties after dark. Ask any property how far it is from the nearest car access and from Jemaa el-Fnaa on foot, and treat vagueness as an answer.

The late-arrival question

If your flight lands after dark on the first night, the medina is at its least forgiving: lanes are quiet, orientation is hard, and luggage is loud. Arrange to be met, in advance, in writing. Travellers who skip this step are the ones with a first-night story, and it is never the story they wanted from the trip.

Which one for a first trip

For a first visit of three or four nights, the medina is the default answer and Gueliz is the sensible alternative for anyone who values calm and predictability over immersion. Families with young children or travellers arriving very late often do best splitting the stay: a couple of nights in the medina for the experience, then somewhere easier. The riad guide explains what you are actually booking.

Where you sleep in Marrakech quietly decides your daily distances, your taxi habit, and how much of the city you meet on foot — which is why it belongs with the sequencing and transport calls rather than on its own. Those connections are laid out in the complete Morocco trip guide.

For what to do once you are settled, see our Marrakech first-timer's guide.

Where to stay in Marrakech: FAQ

Is the medina too noisy?

It can be. Mornings start early and lanes carry sound. Riads with rooms off the courtyard rather than the street are noticeably quieter.

Can a taxi drop me at my riad?

Usually not to the door — cars cannot enter most medina lanes. Good riads meet you at the nearest access point and walk you in.

Is Gueliz a bad choice for a first trip?

Not at all. It trades immersion for comfort and predictability, and it is a short taxi ride from the medina.

Is the Palmeraie worth it?

If you want a resort stay with trips into town, yes. If you plan to spend your evenings in the souks, it is too far out.

How many nights does Marrakech need?

Three or four covers the sights without rushing, and leaves room for a day trip to the Atlas foothills or Essaouira.

title: Riads in Marrakech: How to Choose One (Not Which One)
content:
Choosing a riad in Marrakech is less about finding the single best one than about knowing how to read a listing, because the right riad depends on where in the medina it sits, how easily you reach it, and details a photo will not show. Get the method right and dozens of riads become good choices; get it wrong and a beautiful courtyard turns into a nightly ordeal of stairs and dark lanes. Here is how to choose.

What a riad actually is

A riad is a traditional courtyard house within the medina walls, built inward around a central patio, and staying in one is the classic Marrakech experience — intimate, atmospheric, and a world apart from a modern hotel. The trade is that riads sit inside the pedestrian medina, so cars cannot usually reach the door and rooms in historic buildings vary widely. Understanding that shape is the start of choosing well.

Location within the medina

The most important variable is where in the medina the riad sits, because "in the medina" ranges from a short, clear walk off a main artery to a deep warren of turns that empties after dark. A riad close to a car-accessible point and a recognisable landmark is far easier to live in than one buried six turns deep, however lovely its photos. Ask how far it is from the nearest taxi access and from Jemaa el-Fnaa on foot.

Ask about the arrival

Good riads meet guests at the nearest vehicle point and walk them in, which matters enormously on a first night with luggage in unfamiliar lanes. Confirm this before booking, and arrange the meeting time and place in writing. A riad that leaves you to find it yourself in the dark is telling you something about the stay to come; one that meets you is showing its hospitality from the first minute.

Reading the details that matter

Beyond location, a few details separate a great riad stay from a frustrating one: whether rooms face the courtyard (quieter) or the street (louder, early starts), whether there is a rooftop terrace, how many floors of stairs stand between the entrance and your room, and whether breakfast and airport transfers are included. Historic buildings rarely have lifts, so ask about stairs if that matters to you. These are the things photos flatter and reviews reveal.

Medina riad or easier comfort

The honest trade is immersion against convenience: a medina riad puts you in the heart of the experience with the friction of lanes and stairs, while a hotel in Gueliz or a riad near a medina gate offers easier access and a quieter night. For a first visit of a few nights, most travellers find the medina riad worth every inconvenience; families, late arrivals, or anyone valuing calm may prefer to split the stay. The neighborhood you pick sets the tone before the riad does.

What you're really paying for

Riad prices span an enormous range, and the money mostly buys location, size and service rather than a fundamentally different experience of the courtyard house. A simple, well-run riad in a good spot can beat a lavish one buried deep in the medina, because access and hospitality matter more day to day than thread count. Decide what you actually value — atmosphere, ease, a pool, a rooftop — and pay for that rather than for photos.

Families and longer stays

For families or stays of several nights, the calculus shifts toward practicality: a riad near a medina gate or a hotel in a quieter district can spare you the daily haul of luggage and tired children through the lanes. Some travellers book a medina riad for the first couple of nights and something easier afterward, getting the immersion while it is novel and the comfort when they are worn. Matching the base to the trip's shape is the real skill.

Booking with confidence

Read recent reviews for mentions of the walk-in, the stairs and the noise rather than just the decor, message the riad with your arrival details and any needs, and book directly or through a reputable platform. A short exchange before booking — asking about access, transfers and rooms — tells you as much about the hospitality as any star rating. The riad that answers warmly and clearly is usually the one that looks after you on the ground.

Which riad, and where in the medina, quietly decides your daily walking, your taxi habit and your first-night ease — which is why the base decision belongs with sequencing and transport rather than on its own. How they connect is worked out in the complete Morocco trip guide.

For the neighborhoods, see where to stay in Marrakech; for what riads are in general, our riads explained guide covers the basics.

Choosing a Marrakech riad: FAQ

What's the most important thing to check?

Location within the medina — how far from car access and from Jemaa el-Fnaa on foot. It matters more than the decor.

Will a taxi reach the riad?

Usually not to the door. Good riads meet you at the nearest vehicle point and walk you in — confirm this before booking.

How do I avoid a noisy room?

Ask for a room facing the courtyard rather than the street. Medina mornings start early and sound carries.

Are there lifts in riads?

Rarely — they're historic buildings. Ask how many flights of stairs if that matters to you.

Medina riad or a hotel in Gueliz?

The medina for immersion, Gueliz for easy access and calm. Most first-timers find the riad worth the friction for a few nights.

title: Sahara Desert Camps: Standard, Deluxe, and What Changes
content:
The desert camp is where the price of a Sahara trip really splits, far more than the choice of dune field does, and knowing what separates a standard night from a luxury one lets you spend where it matters to you. The camel ride, the dunes and the stars are shared by every camp; what changes is the comfort of the night in between. Here is what each tier actually gives you.

What a standard camp includes

A standard desert camp is a genuine tented night: a bed in a shared or simple private tent, communal bathroom facilities, a group tagine dinner, and breakfast before the dawn ride out. It is comfortable enough, authentic, and the price most first-timers pay, delivering the whole point of the experience — a night in the dunes — without frills. For many travellers it is exactly right, and the simplicity is part of the appeal.

What luxury adds

A luxury or deluxe camp adds private, en-suite bathrooms, better bedding and larger tents, a quieter and more secluded setting, and often a more elaborate dinner and service. You are paying for comfort and privacy rather than a different view — the dunes and stars are the same. For a honeymoon, a family wanting private facilities, or anyone who sleeps poorly rough, the upgrade is genuinely worth it; for a hardy traveller, it is optional.

The bathroom is the real difference

If one thing decides the tier for most people, it is the bathroom: standard camps share facilities, luxury camps put a private en-suite in your tent. In the desert, that convenience carries more weight than it would in a hotel, and it is the single upgrade travellers most often say they were glad to have paid for. Everything else — bedding, tent size, dinner — is a matter of degree.

What stays the same either way

Every camp, standard or luxury, shares the elements that make the night unforgettable: the camel trek in over the dunes toward sunset, dinner under a vast sky, extraordinary stargazing far from any light, and a sunrise before the drive back. The core experience is remarkably consistent across price points, which is why the standard camp is never a lesser version of the trip — only a simpler bed beneath the same stars.

What to bring for the night

Whatever the tier, a desert night calls for a few specific things: a warm layer for the genuinely cold hours after dark, something long-sleeved to sleep in, a torch or headlamp, and a charged power bank since camps often have no electricity. Standard camps in particular may have limited lighting and no sockets, so arriving prepared makes the simpler night entirely comfortable rather than a test of endurance.

Managing expectations at a standard camp

A standard camp is basic by design, and travellers who expect a hotel in the sand are the ones disappointed, while those who expect a real desert night are delighted by the same camp. Shared facilities, simple food and a canvas tent are the authentic version of the experience, not a shortfall. Knowing that going in is what turns the standard camp from a compromise into exactly the night you came for.

Choosing your tier

Match the camp to who you are travelling as: standard suits budget-minded and adventurous travellers happy to rough it a little, while luxury suits families, couples on a special trip, and anyone who values a private bathroom and a quieter night. Decide this deliberately when you book the tour, since it moves the price as much as the destination does, and it is easy to upgrade at the booking stage and impossible once you are in the dunes.

The camp tier is one of a handful of desert choices — Merzouga or Zagora, from which city, how many nights — that together decide the cost and shape of the whole leg. How they interlock is worked out in the complete Morocco trip guide.

For the destinations, see Merzouga vs Zagora; for how the tours are booked, our Sahara tours guide covers the rest.

Sahara desert camps: FAQ

What does a standard camp include?

A tented bed, shared bathroom facilities, a group tagine dinner and breakfast before the dawn ride. Comfortable and authentic.

What does luxury add?

Private en-suite bathrooms, better bedding, larger tents, a quieter setting and a more elaborate dinner — comfort, not a different view.

Is the upgrade worth it?

For honeymoons, families wanting private facilities, and poor sleepers, yes. For hardy travellers, the standard camp is fine.

What's the same at every camp?

The camel trek, the dunes, dinner under the sky, the stargazing and the sunrise. The core experience is consistent across tiers.

When do I choose the tier?

At booking — it moves the price as much as the destination does, and you cannot upgrade once you are in the dunes.

title: Fez vs. Marrakech: Which to Visit (or Do Both)
content:
Marrakech and Fez are Morocco's two great imperial cities, and first-timers often wonder which to choose — though the honest answer for most trips is both, in sequence. They pull in genuinely different directions: Marrakech is the buzzing, accessible showpiece geared to visitors, while Fez is the older, deeper, more overwhelming medieval maze. Knowing how they differ helps you weight your days even when you see the pair.

Marrakech: the accessible showpiece

Marrakech is the easier introduction to Morocco: its sights are navigable, its tourist infrastructure is extensive, and the energy of Jemaa el-Fnaa and the souks is immediate and thrilling. It is well connected by air and rail, rich in riads and restaurants, and forgiving of a first-timer finding their feet. If you have limited time or want a smoother entry into the country, Marrakech is the natural base.

Who Marrakech suits

Marrakech suits first-timers wanting a vibrant, manageable introduction, travellers on a shorter trip, and anyone using the city as a springboard to the desert, the Atlas or the coast. It is the more comfortable of the two to arrive in cold, and the easier to enjoy without a guide. For many, it is both the start and the hub of a Morocco trip.

Fez: the deeper medieval city

Fez is the older spiritual and cultural heart, and its medina is a larger, more labyrinthine and more intense experience — less polished for tourism, more authentically medieval, and more overwhelming on arrival. It rewards the traveller willing to engage with that intensity, offering a sense of a living historical city that Marrakech, for all its energy, does not quite match. It is the connoisseur's city of the two.

Who Fez suits

Fez suits travellers drawn to history and authenticity over convenience, those on a longer trip with time to go deeper, and anyone who wants the medieval maze at its most genuine. It benefits more from a guided first day than Marrakech does, precisely because it is harder. For a second Moroccan city, or a second trip, it is often the more memorable.

The case for both

On a trip of a week or more, seeing both is the standard and rewarding choice, since they complement rather than repeat each other — the showpiece and the maze, connected directly by train. A common shape is Marrakech and the desert first, then the train north to Fez, absorbing the country's range in one loop. Doing both is less about ticking two boxes than about experiencing two genuinely different Moroccos.

Getting between the two

The practical detail that makes "both" easy is the train: Marrakech and Fez are linked directly by ONCF rail, a comfortable journey of several hours that turns the two cities into the natural endpoints of a single loop. There is no need to double back or arrange a driver — you simply take the train, often via Casablanca. That direct connection is a large part of why seeing both is the standard first-timer plan rather than an ambitious one.

Which order to visit them

Most loops start in Marrakech, because it is the gentler introduction and the usual springboard for the desert, then move north to Fez once you have found your feet. Arriving in Fez first is not wrong, but landing cold in its harder maze asks more of a jet-lagged first-timer. Ending in Fez also lets the trip build from the accessible showpiece toward the deeper, more demanding city, which many find the more satisfying arc.

If you must choose one

Forced to pick, choose Marrakech for a first, shorter, or more cautious trip, and Fez for a deeper, longer, or second visit. Neither is wrong, and the "better" city depends entirely on what you want — ease and energy, or depth and authenticity. Weight your days toward whichever pull is stronger for you, and use the other, if you have time, as the counterpoint that makes both sharper.

Whether you do one city or both, and in what order against the desert and the coast, is a sequencing decision that shapes the whole trip. How the imperial cities fit the loop is worked out in the complete Morocco trip guide.

For each city in depth, see our Marrakech guide and Fez guide.

Fez vs Marrakech: FAQ

Which is better for a first trip?

Marrakech, usually — it's more accessible, better connected, and a smoother introduction. Fez rewards a deeper or second visit.

Should I see both?

On a week or more, yes. They complement each other and are linked directly by train — the showpiece and the medieval maze.

How are they different?

Marrakech is the buzzing, visitor-geared showpiece; Fez is the older, larger, more intense and authentic medieval city.

Which needs a guide more?

Fez. Its medina is a bigger, harder maze, so a guided first day helps more there than in Marrakech.

If I only have time for one?

Marrakech for a shorter or cautious trip; Fez for a longer, history-focused one. Pick by what you want — energy or depth.

title: Sahara Sunrise and Sunset: What the Desert Night Is Like
content:
A night in the Sahara is, for many travelers, the single most memorable part of a Morocco trip — a camel ride out to the dunes at sunset, a night in a desert camp, and a field of stars undimmed by any city light. Knowing what the experience is actually like, from the cold to the rhythm of the evening, helps you arrive prepared and present. Here is what the desert night involves and how to make the most of its two great moments.

Arriving at sunset

The classic arrival is by camel in the late afternoon, riding out from the desert's edge across the dunes as the light turns gold and the sand shifts through ochre and rose — a slow, silent, cinematic entrance to the camp. The camel ride is short and gentle, more atmosphere than adventure, and timed so you reach the dunes for sunset. Climbing a high dune to watch the sun sink over the endless sand is the first of the night's two unforgettable moments.

The camp and the evening

Desert camps range from basic to genuinely luxurious, but the shape of the evening is similar: a tagine dinner eaten communally, often music around a fire under the stars, and the deep quiet of the desert settling in as the temperature drops. It is a sociable, unhurried evening with fellow travelers and the camp's hosts, far from any screen or signal. The simplicity is the point — good food, firelight, and a sky most people have never truly seen.

The stars

With no light pollution for hundreds of miles, the Sahara's night sky is staggering: the Milky Way stretches clear overhead, and the stars are dense and bright in a way that stops conversation. Lying back on the cooling sand to take it in is, for many, the emotional peak of the whole trip. Bring warm layers so you can stay out under the stars comfortably rather than retreating to the tent, and let your eyes adjust fully to the dark.

The cold, and how to prepare

The desert is cold at night year-round and genuinely freezing on winter nights, despite the warm daytime sun, and this surprises unprepared travelers every time. Pack warm layers — a fleece and a jacket even in warmer months, serious warmth in winter — plus a hat and a scarf against the fine sand and the chill. The camps provide heavy blankets, but the evening under the stars is far more pleasant when you have dressed for the cold rather than shivering through it.

What to bring for the night

Beyond warm layers, a few things make the desert night far better: a headlamp or torch for moving around camp in the dark, a fully charged phone or camera (power is scarce, so top up beforehand), a scarf against the sand, and any personal water and medications. The camps provide bedding and meals, so you travel light, but these small items are the difference between a smooth night and a fumbling one. A power bank is especially worth its space here.

Choosing where to go

The desert experience varies by region: Merzouga, with the tall Erg Chebbi dunes, offers the classic towering-sand scenery and is reached via a longer drive, while Zagora is closer to Marrakech but has less dramatic dunes. Which you choose shapes the trip's length and the grandeur of the scenery, so it is worth deciding deliberately rather than taking the first tour offered. For the postcard dunes, Merzouga is the one, and worth the extra driving.

Sunrise, the second gift

Waking before dawn for the desert sunrise is worth the lost sleep: the dunes emerge cold and blue, then flush pink and gold as the sun rises over the sand in near-total silence, a quieter and more private moment than the crowded sunset. Climb a dune, sit still, and watch the desert wake. Then it is mint tea, breakfast, and the camel ride back — but the sunrise, seen by only your small camp, is the memory that tends to last longest of all.

The desert night is the emotional centerpiece that a well-planned trip is built to protect, and how it anchors the route — the days each side, the one-way run to Fez — is worked out in the complete Morocco trip guide.

For the camps themselves, see our desert camps guide; for choosing the region, the Merzouga vs Zagora guide covers it.

The Sahara night: FAQ

What is a night in the desert like?

A camel ride to the dunes at sunset, a communal tagine dinner with music around a fire, an astonishing star field, and a cold, quiet night before a spectacular sunrise.

Is it cold at night?

Yes — cool to cold year-round, freezing on winter nights despite warm days. Pack a fleece and jacket even in warmer months; serious warmth in winter.

How are the stars?

Staggering — no light pollution for hundreds of miles, the Milky Way clear overhead. For many it's the emotional peak of the whole trip.

Is the sunrise worth waking for?

Absolutely — quieter and more private than sunset, with the dunes flushing pink and gold in near-silence. Often the most lasting memory.

What's the camel ride like?

Short and gentle, more atmosphere than adventure, timed to reach the dunes for sunset. The experience, not an endurance test.

title: Alcohol in Morocco: Where You Can and Can't Drink
content:
Alcohol in Morocco is legal but not universal, and knowing where you can and cannot expect a drink saves both awkwardness and false assumptions. This is a Muslim country where most locals do not drink, yet licensed hotels, tourist restaurants and certain shops serve alcohol perfectly openly. The rule is less about legality than about setting and discretion. Here is where a drink is easy, where it is not, and how to handle it respectfully.

Where you can drink

Alcohol is readily available in licensed hotels, upscale and tourist-oriented restaurants, rooftop bars in the cities, and dedicated bars in tourist areas, where wine, beer and spirits are served without fuss. Morocco even produces its own decent wines and a local beer, which you will find on these menus. For a traveller who wants a glass of wine with dinner or a drink on a terrace, the cities make it straightforward.

Where not to expect it

Alcohol is simply absent from most everyday Moroccan life, and that is worth setting expectations around rather than discovering mid-trip. Do not expect it in traditional local restaurants, in the medina's ordinary cafes and eateries, or in more conservative and rural areas, where it is simply not served and asking can be awkward. Most everyday Moroccan dining is alcohol-free, and mint tea or fresh juice is the accompaniment to a meal. This is not a prohibition so much as a cultural default, and matching it where it applies is the courteous move.

Buying alcohol to take away

Beyond bars and restaurants, buying alcohol to drink privately is a common approach for travellers who want a quiet glass without going out. For drinking in your riad or hotel, some supermarkets — notably larger chains like Carrefour and Marjane — have a dedicated alcohol section, and there are specialist liquor shops in the cities. Availability tightens during Ramadan, when sales to Muslims are restricted and some shops limit hours. Buy discreetly, carry it wrapped, and drink it in private rather than in public spaces.

Moroccan wine and beer, briefly

Morocco has a small domestic wine industry centred on the regions around Meknes and Benslimane, producing reds, whites and rosés that appear on hotel and restaurant lists and are perfectly pleasant, and a couple of local lagers fill the beer role. Choosing a Moroccan wine with dinner is both cheaper than an import and a small way into the country's own production. Ask the waiter for the local option and you will usually be pointed to something decent.

Discretion is the whole etiquette

The single guiding principle is discretion: drinking is fine in the settings meant for it and inappropriate in public streets, near mosques, or conspicuously anywhere during Ramadan daylight. Do not carry an open drink through the medina or offer alcohol to locals who may not drink. Keeping it to bars, restaurants and your own accommodation covers every situation and shows the respect the setting asks for.

Drinking in your riad

Many travellers find the easiest approach is a drink in their riad or hotel rather than seeking out bars, buying a bottle discreetly from a supermarket alcohol section and enjoying it on the terrace. Check first that your riad permits it, since some traditional houses prefer guests not to, and keep it low-key regardless. This sidesteps the question of which restaurants serve and keeps everything comfortably private.

During Ramadan

Ramadan tightens everything: alcohol sales to Muslims are restricted, some bars and shops reduce service, and public drinking is especially inappropriate during the fasting month. Licensed tourist hotels generally continue to serve their guests discreetly, so a drink is still available if you want one, but the respectful approach is to keep it low-key and private. As with food, the courtesy is simply not to be conspicuous.

Where alcohol fits — the licensed hotel, the tourist restaurant, the private terrace, never the public street — is one more reading of setting and discretion that runs through a Moroccan trip. Our etiquette guide covers the wider customs, and the food guide covers what to drink instead when alcohol isn't the thing.

Alcohol in Morocco: FAQ

Is alcohol legal in Morocco?

Yes, but not universal. Licensed hotels, tourist restaurants and bars serve it openly; most local eateries and rural areas do not.

Where can I buy it to take away?

Larger supermarkets like Carrefour and Marjane have alcohol sections, plus specialist shops. Buy discreetly and drink in private.

Does Morocco make its own wine?

Yes — decent local wines and a domestic beer, both found on hotel and tourist-restaurant menus.

What about during Ramadan?

Sales to Muslims are restricted and public drinking is especially inappropriate. Licensed tourist hotels still serve guests discreetly.

What's the main rule?

Discretion. Drink in the settings meant for it — bars, restaurants, your accommodation — never in public streets or near mosques.

title: Cooking Classes in Morocco: Worth It and How to Choose
content:
A cooking class is one of the highest-value experiences a first-timer can book in Morocco: a few hours that teach you the dishes, demystify the spices, and send you home able to recreate a tagine, usually for a very reasonable price. The good ones combine a market visit, hands-on cooking and a shared meal, and choosing well is mostly about matching the format to what you want. Here is how they work and what to look for.

What a good class includes

The best cooking classes follow a satisfying arc: a guided visit to a local market to buy fresh ingredients, an explanation of the key spices and techniques, hands-on preparation of a few classic dishes, and then sitting down to eat what you cooked. A class that includes the market trip teaches you as much about Moroccan food culture as about the recipes, and the shared meal at the end is half the pleasure. Look for that full shape rather than a quick demonstration.

The market visit

The market portion is where a class earns its keep beyond the recipes: a good instructor walks you through the spice stalls, the produce and the butchers, showing you what to buy and how, so the souk becomes legible rather than bewildering. For many travellers this is the moment Moroccan food finally makes sense, and it doubles as a gentle, guided introduction to shopping in a market you will otherwise navigate alone. It is worth choosing a class that includes it.

What you'll cook

Most classes teach the staples a first-timer wants to take home: a tagine or two, couscous, Moroccan salads, and often bread or pastries, with mint tea throughout. The dishes are chosen to be reproducible in a home kitchen, and a good instructor sends you off with the recipes and the confidence to make them again. It is the rare souvenir that keeps giving long after the trip, and it travels home in your hands rather than your luggage.

How to choose one

Pick a class by its format and reviews: confirm it includes the market visit and a full hands-on session rather than a watch-and-taste demonstration, check the group size (smaller is more hands-on), and read recent reviews for the quality of the instructor. Riads and hotels often run or recommend well-regarded classes, and booking through your accommodation is an easy, reliable route. Marrakech and Fez both have excellent options.

Classes for families and dietary needs

Cooking classes adapt well to families and to dietary requirements, which makes them a flexible booking: children often enjoy the hands-on element, and vegetarian or other needs are easily accommodated since Moroccan cuisine is rich in vegetable dishes. Mentioning any requirements when you book lets the instructor plan the market trip and menu around them. It is one of the few activities that works for a whole family at once, across ages.

What to expect to pay

A group cooking class is inexpensive for what it delivers — a market trip, hands-on tuition and a full meal — while a private class costs more and buys a tailored menu and pace. Either way the value is high relative to a comparable restaurant meal, since you leave with a skill as well as a full stomach. Booking through a well-reviewed operator or your riad is the simplest way to be sure of quality.

Why it's worth the time

On a packed itinerary a cooking class can feel like a luxury to cut, but it is often the experience travellers remember most warmly: it slows the trip down, teaches a genuine skill, and gives you a direct, hands-on connection to the culture through its food. For the price of a nice dinner, you get a half-day of learning and a meal you made yourself. Few bookings on a Morocco trip return as much for the money.

A cooking class is one of the discretionary experiences that shape the texture of a trip alongside the sights and the desert, and how those choices balance against your days and budget is worked out in the complete Morocco trip guide.

For the dishes you'll learn, see our guide to Moroccan food; for the markets you'll shop, the souk price guide covers the rest.

Morocco cooking classes: FAQ

Are cooking classes worth it?

Yes — one of the best-value experiences for a first-timer. A half-day of learning, a market visit and a meal you cooked, for the price of a nice dinner.

What does a good class include?

A guided market visit, an explanation of spices and techniques, hands-on cooking of a few classics, and sitting down to eat what you made.

What will I cook?

Usually a tagine, couscous, Moroccan salads and often bread or pastries, with mint tea — staples chosen to reproduce at home.

How do I choose one?

Confirm it includes the market visit and full hands-on cooking, check the group size, and read recent reviews. Riads often recommend good ones.

Where are the best classes?

Marrakech and Fez both have excellent options, easily booked through your riad or hotel.

title: Mint Tea in Morocco: The Ritual and the Etiquette
content:
Mint tea is the constant companion of a Moroccan trip: offered in shops, homes, riads and at every pause, it is a gesture of hospitality woven through daily life across North Africa. For a first-timer the ritual can be slightly bewildering — when to accept, whether it obligates you, why it is poured from such a height — and understanding it makes every encounter smoother. Here is what the tea means and how to navigate it gracefully.

What it is

The tea is green tea brewed with fresh spearmint and a generous amount of sugar, served in small glasses rather than cups, and it is drunk throughout the day, not just after meals. Sweet, hot and aromatic, it is central to social life across the Maghreb, and Morocco has its own beloved version. The sugar is traditional and heavy; if you prefer it less sweet, you can ask, though the classic serving is frankly sweet.

The pouring ritual

You will notice the tea poured from a height, a long stream from pot to glass, and this is deliberate: it aerates the tea, creates a light foam on top, and is a small performance of hospitality and skill. The host may pour the first glass back into the pot to mix it before serving. Watching the pour is part of the pleasure, and a well-executed one from height is a point of pride for the person serving.

The etiquette of accepting

When tea is offered — in a home, a riad, or a shop — accepting is the gracious response, as it is a genuine gesture of welcome, and sharing a glass is a small act of connection rather than a commitment to anything. In a carpet or craft shop, though, be aware that the tea is also part of the sales ritual: accepting it is fine and does not obligate you to buy, but understand that the hospitality and the sales pitch are intertwined. You can enjoy the tea and still decline the goods.

Can you refuse?

Refusing tea is not catastrophic, but accepting is warmer, and if you genuinely cannot — time, too much sugar already — a polite, appreciative decline is understood. In a home especially, accepting at least a glass honours the hospitality. The tea is offered in a spirit of generosity, and meeting it in the same spirit, even briefly, is the graceful path. A flat refusal can read as cold in a culture where the offer means a great deal.

Tea in the shop, plainly

Because mint tea appears the moment you show interest in a carpet or craft shop, it is worth naming the dynamic: the glass is real hospitality and a softening ritual before the negotiation, both at once. Accept it if you like, enjoy it, and keep a clear head about the separate question of whether and what to buy. The tea creates a warm obligation by design, and knowing that lets you receive the warmth without being moved by the obligation.

Tea beyond the shop

Away from the commerce, the tea is simply lovely: offered by a riad on arrival, poured at the end of a meal, shared on a rooftop as the call to prayer sounds, it punctuates the day with small warm pauses. Cafes serve it all day, and a pot with a plate of pastries is one of the cheapest and most pleasant ways to rest between sights. Learning to enjoy it unhurried is learning something real about the pace of the place.

Making it at home

Many travellers take the ritual home, buying a pot, glasses and green tea in the souks to recreate it, and a cooking class often teaches the proper method — the brewing, the sugar, the pour from height. It is an inexpensive, evocative souvenir that carries the trip into your kitchen. If you want to buy the kit, the souks have every grade of teapot and glass, and bargaining applies as it does to any craft purchase.

Making it part of the trip

The best approach is to lean into the ritual: accept the tea when it is offered in good faith, learn to enjoy its sweetness, and treat each glass as the small human moment it is meant to be. It is one of the genuine warmths of travelling in Morocco, and the pauses over tea — on a rooftop, in a shop, in someone's home — are often what travellers remember most fondly. Just keep the shop version's dual nature in mind.

The tea ritual is inseparable from the shop encounter and the wider hospitality that shapes every interaction, and how that warmth and the commerce beneath it fit together is worked out in the complete Morocco trip guide.

For the shop context, see our carpet shop guide; for the broader customs, the etiquette guide covers it.

Mint tea in Morocco: FAQ

What is Moroccan mint tea?

Green tea brewed with fresh spearmint and plenty of sugar, served hot in small glasses throughout the day — a gesture of hospitality across North Africa.

Why is it poured from height?

To aerate the tea and create a light foam on top — a small performance of hospitality and skill.

Does accepting tea in a shop obligate me to buy?

No. The tea is real hospitality and part of the sales ritual at once. Enjoy it, and decide separately whether to buy.

Can I refuse the tea?

Yes, politely — but accepting is warmer, especially in a home, where it honours the hospitality. A flat refusal can read as cold.

Can I ask for less sugar?

You can, though the classic serving is frankly sweet. The heavy sugar is traditional.

title: Morocco for First-Timers: Everything You Need to Know Before You Go
content:
Morocco is one of those places that feels impossibly far from home and then, three hours after landing, feels like somewhere you've always wanted to be. For a first-time American traveler, it's an easy introduction to North Africa and the Arab world: it's set up for tourism, the distances are manageable, and you can pack sweeping desert, medieval cities, and Atlantic beaches into a single trip. This guide covers the things first-timers actually worry about, so you can plan with confidence rather than guesswork.

Do Americans need a visa for Morocco?

No. U.S. citizens can enter Morocco visa-free for tourism and stay up to 90 days. You'll get a stamp on arrival; there's no fee and no online application to fill out beforehand. That said, entry rules are the one thing worth double-checking close to your trip, since governments change them without much notice. Make sure your passport is valid for at least six months beyond your entry date and has a blank page for the stamp. We cover the details in our Morocco visa guide for Americans.

Is Morocco safe?

For the vast majority of visitors, yes. Violent crime against tourists is rare, and Morocco is generally considered one of the safer countries in the region — millions of travelers, including solo women, visit every year without incident. What you'll actually deal with is petty stuff: pickpocketing in crowds, aggressive touts, and medina scams like a stranger insisting a street is "closed" so they can lead you somewhere. None of it is dangerous, but it's worth knowing about so it doesn't rattle you. Our honest safety guide walks through it, and the common scams are easy to sidestep once you know the playbook.

Money: the dirham is a closed currency

The Moroccan dirham is a closed currency, so you cannot buy it before you fly — no US bank sells it. You withdraw dirham from an ATM once you land (there are machines in the Casablanca and Marrakech arrival halls) or change dollars at a licensed bureau. Morocco runs heavily on cash: souks, taxis and small cafes are cash-only, while hotels and nicer restaurants take cards.

When should you visit?

Spring (March to May) and fall (September to November) are the sweet spots: warm days, cool nights, and comfortable conditions for both the cities and the desert. Summer gets brutally hot inland — Marrakech, Fez, and the Sahara can push past 100°F — though the coast at Essaouira stays mild. Winter is cool and pleasant in the cities, cold at night in the desert, and snowy in the Atlas Mountains. If your dates overlap Ramadan, the rhythm of daily life changes; it's a fascinating time to visit but worth understanding first. See our month-by-month guide.

Where to go on a first trip

A first trip usually covers four places in ten days or fewer: Marrakech as the entry point, Fez for the medieval medina, Chefchaouen in the Rif mountains, and one night in the Sahara. Each is completely different from the last, and the distances between them shape the itinerary more than the sights do. The classic loop, in order:

Marrakech

The sensory heart of Morocco and the usual starting point, with the famous Jemaa el-Fnaa square, endless souks, and gorgeous gardens. See our Marrakech guide.

Fez

Home to the world's largest car-free medieval city — a genuine maze where a local guide for the first day pays for itself.

Chefchaouen

The blue-washed mountain town, small, relaxed, and endlessly photogenic.

The Sahara

A night in a desert camp among the dunes of Erg Chebbi is the bucket-list experience — camel ride at sunset, dinner under the stars, sunrise over the sand.

Essaouira and the Atlas Mountains

A windswept Atlantic beach town and the Berber villages of the High Atlas round out the trip if you have time.

Getting around

Morocco is easier to navigate than you'd expect. Comfortable ONCF trains connect Casablanca, Rabat, Fez, and Marrakech, with a high-speed line up north. For places off the rail network — Chefchaouen, Essaouira, and the desert gateways — CTM and Supratours coaches are the reliable options. In cities, small metered "petit taxis" handle short hops (insist on the meter or agree the fare first). The Sahara is almost always done as a multi-day tour with a driver. More in our transport guide.

Language: will you get by?

Yes. Arabic and Tamazight (Berber) are the official languages, and French is widely spoken in business, government, and tourism — a legacy you'll notice on signs and menus. In the places tourists spend time, English is common: hotel and riad staff, guides, and popular restaurants will usually handle English fine. Away from the tourist track, a few words of French go further than English, and any attempt at Arabic — a simple "salam" (hello) or "shukran" (thank you) — is warmly received. You don't need to speak the language to travel here comfortably, but a handful of phrases makes every interaction friendlier.

What a first trip actually feels like

Set your expectations for contrast, because that's the Morocco experience. One hour you're haggling for a lantern in a chaotic souk with a dozen smells competing for your attention; the next you're sipping tea in silent riad courtyard. The cities are intense and can be tiring — the constant sensory input and the occasional tout wear on you — so build in downtime and don't try to cram every day full. The desert and mountains, by contrast, are serene. A well-paced first trip alternates the two, and most people leave already planning a return.

Practical first-timer tips

A few things that smooth out a first trip: dress modestly, especially outside tourist zones — covering shoulders and knees is respectful and also helps with sun and heat. Get an eSIM so you land connected, which is handy when you need maps or a ride the moment you arrive and don't have dirham yet. Accept the mint tea when it's offered; it's hospitality, not a sales trap. And decide early whether you want a guided tour or independent travel — both work well here, and it shapes how you book everything else. The connections between these decisions — base, route, desert, money — are worked out together in the complete Morocco trip guide.

Morocco first-timer FAQ

How many days do you need for a first trip to Morocco?

Seven days covers a solid taste (two cities plus a desert night); ten days is the comfortable classic loop; two weeks lets you add the coast and mountains without rushing.

Can you drink alcohol in Morocco?

Yes — it's legal for tourists and served in many hotels, licensed restaurants, and bars, though it's not consumed openly in public. It's simply less visible than at home.

Do people speak English in Morocco?

Arabic and Tamazight are official, and French is widely used. English is common in tourist areas — hotels, guides, and popular restaurants — though a few French or Arabic phrases go a long way elsewhere.

Is Morocco good for a first international trip?

It's a great step beyond Europe: exotic and different, but well set up for tourists, with short distances and plenty of infrastructure. A little preparation goes a long way.

title: Jemaa el-Fnaa: How to Do the Square Without Getting Fleeced
content:
Jemaa el-Fnaa is the beating heart of Marrakech and, at dusk, one of the great spectacles of travel — a vast square that fills with food stalls, musicians, storytellers and crowds as the light fades. It is also mildly predatory in the practiced way of famous tourist squares, and knowing the handful of small traps in advance lets you give yourself over to the theatre of the place without being quietly overcharged for it. Here is how to do the square well.

What the square is

By day Jemaa el-Fnaa is a relatively open plaza with juice carts and a few performers; by evening it transforms into a dense, smoky carnival of food stalls, gnaoua musicians, storytellers and henna artists that is the single most atmospheric hour in Marrakech. The right way to experience it is simply to arrive around sunset, walk in slowly, and let the energy build around you. It is free to wander, and the wandering is the point.

Time your visit for dusk

The square is at its most magical as the sun sets and the food stalls assemble, so aim to arrive in the late afternoon and stay into the evening. A rooftop cafe on the edge gives you the panoramic view first — worth the price of a mint tea — before you descend into the crowd itself. Seeing it from above and then from within is the ideal sequence for a first night.

The small traps, and how they work

A few practiced approaches run on the square, all of them commercial rather than dangerous: henna artists who take your hand and begin before you agree a price, animal handlers who place a monkey or a snake on you and then demand payment, and performers who expect a tip if you so much as photograph them. None is a threat; each works by creating a small obligation you did not consent to. Keep your hands to yourself, decline anything placed on you, and agree any price before, not after.

Photography costs money here

Photographing the performers, water-sellers in their bright costumes, or animal handlers is expected to come with a tip, and snapping without asking reliably produces a demand. Either agree a small payment first or shoot the scene wide without singling anyone out. This is one place where the "ask before photographing people" rule is not just courtesy but a way to avoid a confrontation over money.

Eating at the food stalls

The numbered food stalls that fill the square at night are a genuine experience and mostly good, but the busiest tourist ones pad the bill with unordered extras — bread, olives, dips that arrive unbidden and appear on the tab. Choose a stall busy with locals as well as visitors, confirm what you are ordering, and wave away anything you did not ask for as it lands. Check the bill against what you actually had, and the meal is both cheap and excellent.

Freshly squeezed juice

The orange juice carts are a square institution and inexpensive, though it is worth confirming the price and asking for it without ice if your stomach is cautious. They are a pleasant, low-risk way to take part in the square by day, when the food stalls have not yet assembled. A quick price check before you order heads off the occasional inflated tourist quote.

Enjoying it without the stress

The whole square reduces to a simple posture: arrive at dusk, walk in relaxed, keep your hands and your camera to yourself unless you have agreed a price, pick a busy stall and confirm your order, and let the rest wash over you. Handled that way, Jemaa el-Fnaa is not a gauntlet but one of the most alive places you will stand in on the whole trip. The traps are small; the spectacle is enormous.

The square's small overcharges are the same opening-price habit that runs through the souk and the taxi rank — a first number that assumes you do not know better. How that one habit connects the whole trip is worked out in the complete Morocco trip guide.

For the food stalls in the wider context, see our street food guide; for the souks beside the square, the souk price guide covers bargaining.

Jemaa el-Fnaa: FAQ

When should I visit the square?

At dusk, when the food stalls assemble and the square transforms. Arrive late afternoon and stay into the evening.

What are the traps?

Henna started before you agree a price, animals placed on you for payment, and tips demanded for photos. All commercial, none dangerous — agree prices first.

Can I photograph the performers?

Only with a tip agreed first. Snapping without asking reliably produces a demand for money.

Are the food stalls safe and fair?

Mostly good — pick a busy one, confirm your order, and wave away unordered extras that pad the bill. Check the tab at the end.

Is the orange juice worth it?

Yes, cheap and a square institution. Confirm the price and skip the ice if your stomach is sensitive.

title: Chefchaouen: What to Do in the Blue City
content:
Chefchaouen, the blue-washed town in the Rif Mountains, is Morocco's most photogenic place and one of its most relaxed — a small, walkable medina where nearly every lane and wall is painted a shade of cornflower blue. It is a change of pace from the intensity of Fez and Marrakech, and a day or two is plenty to enjoy it fully. Here is what to do in the blue city, where the best views are, and how to get there.

Wander the blue medina

The main thing to do in Chefchaouen is simply to wander: the blue-painted medina is compact, safe and made for aimless strolling, with photogenic corners, plant-filled doorways and painted staircases around every turn. Unlike the great city medinas, this one is small enough that you cannot really get lost, and gentle enough that the hassle is minimal. Give yourself an unhurried morning to drift through the lanes with a camera and no agenda — that is the town at its best.

The best photo spots

Chefchaouen rewards photographers, and a few spots stand out: the stepped, plant-draped alleys of the upper medina, the doorways framed in contrasting blues, and the Plaza Uta el-Hammam with its kasbah and mosque at the center. Early morning gives you empty lanes and soft light before the day-trippers arrive; the blue glows most in the gentle hours. Respect residents' privacy and homes as you shoot — this is a living town, not a set.

The Spanish Mosque viewpoint

For the classic panorama, walk up to the Spanish Mosque on the hillside opposite the medina, a short uphill hike rewarded by a sweeping view over the whole blue town cradled in the mountains — spectacular at sunset. It is the one bit of exertion the town asks of you, and worth timing for the golden hour when the light softens and the blue deepens. Bring water for the climb and arrive early for a good sunset spot, as it is popular.

Beyond the blue

Chefchaouen sits in the green Rif Mountains, so beyond the medina there are walks and nature close by: the Ras el-Maa waterfall at the medina's edge where locals gather, and trails into the surrounding hills, including toward Akchour and its waterfalls for those wanting a proper day hike. The town also has a relaxed cafe culture perfect for whiling away an afternoon. It rewards a slower stay than its size suggests, if you have the days to give it.

Shopping and local crafts

Chefchaouen has a relaxed, low-pressure shopping scene compared with the big-city souks, known for wool goods, blankets, and locally made crafts in the town's signature blues. The hassle is minimal and the atmosphere gentle, making it a pleasant place to browse and buy without the hard sell of Fez or Marrakech. Bargaining still applies but is softer here; a fair, friendly negotiation gets you a good price on a genuine memento of the blue city.

Where to eat with a view

The town's rooftop terraces and Plaza Uta el-Hammam cafes are made for lingering, with simple Moroccan fare and mountain views over the blue rooftops. Meals are inexpensive and unhurried, and a rooftop dinner as the town lights come on is one of Chefchaouen's quiet pleasures. It is not a destination for elaborate dining, but for a relaxed tagine with a view, it more than delivers.

How to get there

Chefchaouen is not on the rail network, so you reach it by bus (CTM or Supratours) or private transfer, most commonly from Fez, which is the nearest major hub at a few hours away. Many visitors come as an overnight from Fez or fold it into a northern loop. The mountain road is scenic; book the popular Fez coach a day or two ahead in high season. Once there, the town is entirely walkable and needs no transport.

Chefchaouen is the kind of restful counterpoint that shapes the rhythm of a longer trip, and whether to fit it in — and against what — is one of the routing choices the fuller plan weighs. How the blue city fits a northern loop is worked out in the complete Morocco trip guide.

For reaching it, see our getting to Chefchaouen guide; for the coaches, the CTM vs Supratours guide covers the buses.

Things to do in Chefchaouen: FAQ

What is there to do in Chefchaouen?

Wander the blue medina, photograph the painted lanes, hike to the Spanish Mosque viewpoint, and enjoy the relaxed cafe culture. A day or two is plenty.

Where are the best photos?

The stepped upper-medina alleys, contrasting blue doorways, and the Spanish Mosque panorama at sunset. Go early for empty lanes and soft light.

Is there anything beyond the medina?

Yes — the Ras el-Maa waterfall at the medina's edge and hikes into the Rif Mountains, including toward Akchour's waterfalls for a full day out.

How do I get to Chefchaouen?

By bus (CTM or Supratours) or private transfer, most often from Fez, a few hours away. It's not on the train network.

How long should I stay?

A day or two. It's small and walkable, but its relaxed pace and nearby hikes reward a slower stay if you have the time.

title: Marrakech for First-Timers: The Complete Guide
content:
Marrakech is where most first trips to Morocco begin, and for good reason — it's the country's sensory heart, a swirl of souks, palaces, gardens, and one of the most famous squares on earth. It can also be gloriously overwhelming on day one. This guide sets you up to enjoy Marrakech rather than just survive it.

Getting to Marrakech

You can fly straight into Marrakech Menara (RAK), which is what most first-timers doing the classic loop do — it saves the transfer from Casablanca. If you land at Casablanca instead, a comfortable ONCF train reaches Marrakech in about three hours. The airport is only about fifteen minutes from the medina; arrange a pickup through your riad for the smoothest arrival, since finding a specific riad in the medina maze with luggage is the one genuinely tricky first-day moment. Our flights guide covers routing from the U.S.

The top things to see

Marrakech's essential sights sit close together: Jemaa el-Fnaa and the souks immediately north of it, the Koutoubia minaret on the square's western edge, and the Bahia Palace and Saadian Tombs to the south. The Majorelle Garden is the one that needs a taxi. Two full days covers all of it without rushing, which leaves room for the aimless wandering that makes the city. The essentials:

Jemaa el-Fnaa

The legendary main square — sleepy by day, electric at dusk when food stalls, musicians, and storytellers take over. Watch it fill up from a rooftop cafe with a mint tea, then dive in.

The souks

The labyrinth of markets north of the square, selling everything from lanterns and leather to spices and rugs. Getting lost here is the point; haggling is expected (our haggling guide helps).

Palaces and gardens

The ornate Bahia Palace, the serene Saadian Tombs, the historic Ben Youssef Madrasa with its dazzling tilework, and the cobalt-blue Majorelle Garden (and the adjacent YSL museum) for a calm, green break. The Koutoubia minaret anchors the skyline — you can admire it from outside, though the mosque itself isn't open to non-Muslims.

For a fuller run-down, see our dedicated things to do in Marrakech.

Where to stay

Your base shapes the whole experience. The classic choice is a riad in the medina — steps from the action, atmospheric, and a quiet courtyard retreat from the bustle. If you'd rather have modern hotels, restaurants, and easier logistics, Gueliz (the Ville Nouvelle) is the modern district; Hivernage is upscale and quieter; and the Palmeraie offers resort-style stays outside the center. Most first-timers pick a medina riad for the atmosphere. Our where to stay in Marrakech guide breaks down the areas.

Day trips from Marrakech

Marrakech is the launchpad for some of Morocco's best excursions. The Ourika Valley and Atlas foothills are an easy 1–1.5 hours out for Berber villages and waterfalls; the Agafay stone desert offers a close sunset-camp experience without the long desert drive; Essaouira on the coast makes a good full-day escape; and the Sahara at Merzouga is the big one — a multi-day guided trip (see our Sahara tours from Marrakech guide).

Handling the hustle

Marrakech is friendly but also the most touristed city in Morocco, which means touts, faux guides, and the occasional scam. None of it is dangerous — a firm, polite "la shukran" (no thank you) and walking on handles most of it. Ignore anyone insisting a street or sight is "closed," agree taxi fares before getting in, and settle a price before any photo with a performer. Our safety guide preps you fully. Go in expecting a bit of theater and it becomes part of the fun rather than a stressor.

Getting around Marrakech

The medina is car-free and best explored on foot — expect to walk a lot, and wear comfortable shoes for the uneven lanes. For longer hops (to Gueliz, the Majorelle Garden, or the train station), small metered petit taxis are cheap; insist on the meter or agree the fare first, as some drivers will claim it's broken. Horse-drawn carriages (calèches) are a touristy but pleasant way to loop the ramparts. Ride-hail apps operate in the city too. One tip: note a nearby landmark or gate for your riad, because GPS struggles in the dense medina and you'll navigate the last stretch on foot by feel.

Eating in Marrakech

Marrakech is a fantastic place to eat, from street food to refined rooftop dining. Start with the Jemaa el-Fnaa food stalls for atmosphere (choose busy ones), graduate to rooftop riad restaurants for tagine with a view, and seek out the modern Moroccan spots in Gueliz for a calmer sit-down meal. Don't miss street classics like fresh orange juice from the square, msemen (flaky pancakes) at breakfast, and a pastry with mint tea in the afternoon. A cooking class or food tour is a great way to go deeper — our guide to Moroccan dishes tells you what to order.

Best time to visit Marrakech

Marrakech is at its best in spring (March–May) and fall (September–November), when days are warm and evenings pleasant. Summer is intensely hot — often over 100°F — which makes midday sightseeing tough, though early mornings, late evenings, and shady riad courtyards with plunge pools help. Winter days are mild and sunny but nights get cold, so pack layers. The city runs year-round, but timing your visit for the shoulder seasons makes the walking, the souks, and the day trips far more comfortable; see our when-to-go guide for the full picture.

How long to stay

Two to three days is right for a first visit — enough for the sights, the souks, an evening or two at Jemaa el-Fnaa, and a day trip. It's also the natural starting point before heading to the desert and Fez, as laid out in our 10-day itinerary. Give the city a relaxed first day to acclimate, and let the medina reveal itself slowly. How Marrakech fits the wider route is covered in the complete Morocco trip guide.

Marrakech FAQ

How many days do you need in Marrakech?

Two to three days covers the main sights, the souks, Jemaa el-Fnaa, and a day trip — and it's the ideal launch point for the desert and Fez.

Where should first-timers stay in Marrakech?

Most choose a riad in the medina for the atmosphere and central location. Gueliz suits those who prefer modern hotels and easier logistics.

Is Marrakech safe for tourists?

Yes, with normal precautions. The main issues are touts and scams, not danger — a polite refusal and settling prices in advance handle most of it.

What's the best day trip from Marrakech?

The Atlas Mountains (Ourika Valley) for an easy day out, or a multi-day Sahara tour to Merzouga for the bucket-list desert night.

title: Best Things to Do in Marrakech
content:
Marrakech packs an enormous amount into a compact old city, and a first-timer can easily fill two or three days without repeating a thing. Here are the best things to do, from the unmissable icons to the smaller pleasures that make the city special.

Experience Jemaa el-Fnaa at dusk

The city's beating heart and the thing to do first. By day it's a wide, sun-baked square with juice stalls and snake charmers; at sunset it transforms into a carnival of food stalls, musicians, and storytellers. The move is to watch it fill up from a rooftop terrace cafe with a mint tea, then descend into the crowd. Eat at a busy food stall, keep an eye on your belongings, and soak up an atmosphere that's been going for centuries.

Get lost in the souks

The maze of covered markets stretching north from the square is a highlight in itself. Each area specializes — leather, lanterns, spices, carpets, metalwork — and haggling is expected and part of the fun (our haggling guide gives you the playbook). Don't over-plan; wandering and getting pleasantly lost is exactly the right way to experience them.

Tour the palaces and historic sites

Marrakech's architecture is stunning up close. The Bahia Palace is a 19th-century showpiece of painted ceilings and courtyards. The Saadian Tombs hide dazzling tilework behind a narrow passage. The Ben Youssef Madrasa, a former Quranic school, is one of the most beautiful buildings in the country. And the Koutoubia minaret — the city's tallest landmark — anchors the skyline, best admired from outside as the mosque is closed to non-Muslims.

Find calm in the gardens

When the medina's intensity gets to you, the gardens are the antidote. The Majorelle Garden, painted its famous cobalt blue, is a cool botanical oasis, with the Yves Saint Laurent museum next door. The Menara Gardens and Le Jardin Secret offer more green respite. These make perfect mid-afternoon breaks from the heat and the crowds.

Soak in a hammam

A traditional hammam (steam bath and scrub) is a quintessential North African experience and a wonderful way to unwind after days of walking. Options range from local public hammams to luxurious spa versions in riads and hotels — first-timers often prefer the gentler spa route. It's relaxing, cultural, and leaves you feeling brand new. First-timers should know the basic ritual: you'll steam to soften the skin, get scrubbed with black soap and a coarse glove (kessa) that removes astonishing amounts of dead skin, rinse, and often finish with an argan-oil massage. In a public hammam you bring your own toiletries and it's gender-separated; in a spa version everything is provided and it's more pampering than authentic. Either way, it's an experience worth having at least once.

Take a cooking class or food tour

Moroccan cuisine is a trip highlight, and a hands-on cooking class — often starting with a souk shopping trip — teaches you to make tagine and other staples while demystifying the ingredients. Food tours of the medina are another great way to eat well and understand what you're tasting. Our guide to Moroccan dishes tells you what to look for.

Escape on a day trip

If you have an extra day, Marrakech is the springboard for great excursions — the Atlas foothills and Ourika Valley for mountain scenery, the Agafay desert for a close sunset-camp experience, or Essaouira on the coast. The big one, of course, is a multi-day trip to the Sahara; see our Sahara tours guide.

Shop for Moroccan crafts

Marrakech is one of the best places in the country to shop, and the crafts are genuinely special: hand-knotted rugs, leather bags and poufs, brass and silver lanterns, ceramics, babouche slippers, and argan-oil products. Prices are almost always negotiable, so haggling is expected — start well below the asking price and settle somewhere in the middle, always with good humor. If big-ticket items like rugs feel intimidating, the fixed-price artisan cooperatives (Ensemble Artisanal) are a low-pressure way to gauge fair prices before you dive into the souks. Our haggling guide walks through the etiquette.

Watch a sunset from the ramparts or a rooftop

Marrakech glows at golden hour. The city's red-earth walls and the palm groves take on a warm light, and a rooftop terrace above the medina — mint tea in hand, the call to prayer echoing across the rooftops, the Atlas Mountains sometimes visible in the distance — is one of those simple travel moments that stays with you. Many riads and cafes have rooftop terraces open to the public; it's the perfect way to bookend a busy day of sightseeing before heading down to Jemaa el-Fnaa for the evening.

Day and evening rhythm

A smart way to structure a Marrakech day is to work with the heat and the city's rhythm rather than against it. Sightsee the palaces, madrasas, and gardens in the cooler morning hours, retreat to your riad or a shady cafe for lunch and a rest during the hottest part of the afternoon, then re-emerge in the late afternoon for the souks and a rooftop sunset before Jemaa el-Fnaa comes alive at dusk. This gentle pacing keeps you from burning out — the city is intense, and trying to power through midday heat is how first-timers end up exhausted by day two. Build in the downtime and you'll enjoy it far more.

Enjoy the rooftops

Some of Marrakech's best moments are simply sitting on a rooftop terrace above the medina — a coffee in the morning, a sunset drink, dinner overlooking the square. Many riads and cafes have them, and they offer a calm bird's-eye view of a city that's anything but calm at street level. Plan your visit around our complete Marrakech guide. Which of these earn a ticket and which reward a wander is worked through in the complete Morocco trip guide.

Things to do in Marrakech FAQ

What is Marrakech best known for?

The Jemaa el-Fnaa square, its sprawling souks, ornate palaces and gardens, and as the launch point for Atlas and Sahara excursions.

What should you not miss in Marrakech?

Jemaa el-Fnaa at dusk, the souks, the Bahia Palace and Ben Youssef Madrasa, the Majorelle Garden, and a traditional hammam.

Is two days enough for Marrakech?

Two days covers the essentials; three lets you add a hammam, a cooking class, or a day trip at a relaxed pace.

What's a good rainy-day or heat-break activity?

A hammam, a cooking class, or the gardens and museums — all pleasant escapes from midday heat or the occasional wet day.

title: Fez for First-Timers: The Complete Guide
content:
If Marrakech is Morocco's showman, Fez is its scholar — older, deeper, and more traditional. Home to the world's largest car-free urban area, Fez is a living medieval city that many travelers end up loving even more than Marrakech. It's also the most bewildering to navigate, so a little preparation goes a long way.

Getting to Fez

Fez is well connected: comfortable ONCF trains run from Casablanca, Rabat, and Marrakech, or you can fly into Fez–Saïss (FEZ), useful if you're running the classic loop in reverse.
