If your itinerary is genuinely one-way, price the fee into the comparison against train-plus-driver, which sometimes wins outright once the extras are counted.

The honest recommendation

For most first trips, the answer is not to self-drive: take the train between the imperial cities, use a tour or driver for the desert, and consider a rental only if a specific leg — the Atlas, the coast — genuinely calls for one. Save the car for the part of the trip where freedom of movement is the whole point, and let easier modes carry the rest.

Whether a leg goes by car, train, coach or driver is one strand of the sequencing that decides how a whole trip flows and where you can base — a call worked out in the complete Morocco trip guide. Our transport overview covers every mode together, and the Atlas Mountains guide covers the drive a car is actually for.

Renting a car in Morocco: FAQ

Should I rent a car for a first trip?

Usually not. Take the train between cities and a tour or driver for the desert. Rent only for a specific scenic leg like the Atlas or the coast.

Can I drive on my US license?

Yes, for short stays, with an International Driving Permit recommended alongside it. Morocco drives on the right.

Is hiring a driver better?

Often, yes — it costs less than expected and removes traffic, parking and checkpoints while adding an informal guide. A sweet spot for the desert and country routes.

Are police checkpoints a problem?

No. They are common and routine. Have documents ready, be polite, and they pass without issue.

Is night driving safe?

Not really — livestock, pedestrians and unlit vehicles make it risky. Plan to arrive before dark.

title: Getting to Chefchaouen: Every Route from Fez and Tangier
content:
Chefchaouen catches first-timers out because the blue city sits in the Rif mountains with no train line, so the smooth ONCF rail that carries you between the other cities simply stops short of it. Reaching it means a coach or a shared taxi, and knowing the routes in advance keeps this leg from becoming the awkward gap in an otherwise easy itinerary. Here is every way in and how it fits a trip.

Why there's no train

Chefchaouen is not on Morocco's rail network, and no line reaches the Rif mountains where it sits, so any plan that assumes a train there will fail. This is the single fact to absorb before routing a trip through the blue city: you arrive by road, from Fez or Tangier, by coach or grand taxi. Building the leg around that reality rather than discovering it late is the whole trick.

From Fez: the common route

The most common approach is the coach from Fez, a scenic mountain journey of roughly four hours run by reliable operators like CTM and Supratours. It is comfortable, inexpensive and the standard way first-timers arrive, pairing naturally with a Fez stay earlier in the loop. Book a day or two ahead in high season, since seats on the popular departures fill and the schedule is not frequent.

Booking the coach

CTM and Supratours sell tickets online and at their stations, and reserving ahead secures a seat on the timing you want rather than leaving you to the next departure hours later. Arrive with a little time in hand, keep the ticket for the journey, and treat the mountain scenery as part of the experience rather than dead transit. It is one of the prettier legs of a Moroccan trip.

From Tangier

Chefchaouen is also reachable from Tangier in a couple of hours by coach or grand taxi, which suits trips that start in the north or combine the blue city with the Tangier region. This routing works well if you are arriving by ferry from Spain or flying into the north, letting you take in Chefchaouen before heading south to Fez and beyond. The road is shorter than from Fez but the principle is the same: no rail, so coach or taxi.

The grand taxi option

Shared grand taxis run these routes too, leaving when full and priced per seat, and they are faster and more flexible than the coach if you do not mind the shared-sedan format. You can also charter a whole taxi for a private, immediate departure at roughly six times the seat fare — a reasonable choice for a group or a family wanting to leave on their own schedule. Agree the per-seat or whole-car price before you set off.

How long the journey really takes

The Fez route runs about four hours by coach and the Tangier route around two, and treating those as half-day commitments each way is the honest way to plan. Adding the wait for a scheduled departure and the transfer to your riad, a travel day to or from Chefchaouen is a travel day, not a morning. Planning it as such — arriving with the afternoon free rather than the whole day gone to logistics — keeps the leg from feeling like a slog.

Onward from the blue city

Leaving Chefchaouen follows the same rules in reverse: coach or grand taxi back to Fez or on to Tangier, with the same advice to book ahead in high season. If the blue city is your northern turnaround, plan the onward leg before you arrive so a relaxing stay does not end in a scramble for the last seat out. The mountains reward planning the exit as carefully as the entrance.

How it fits a loop

Chefchaouen slots most naturally between Fez and the north, added as a two-night detour rather than squeezed into a day, since the mountain journey each way eats real time. A common shape is Marrakech and the desert first, then Fez, then the coach up to Chefchaouen, then onward or back. Treating it as a restful pause in the mountains, not a rushed tick-box, is how the blue city rewards the effort of reaching it.

The Chefchaouen leg is a clean example of sequencing mattering: a place off the rail line reshapes the order and pace of a whole trip. How the blue city fits with the desert, Fez and the rest is worked out in the complete Morocco trip guide.

For the town itself, see our Chefchaouen guide; for the transport network overall, the transport overview covers coaches and taxis.

Getting to Chefchaouen: FAQ

Is there a train to Chefchaouen?

No. It sits in the Rif mountains with no rail line. You arrive by coach or grand taxi from Fez or Tangier.

How do I get there from Fez?

A scenic coach of about four hours with CTM or Supratours — the common route. Book a day or two ahead in high season.

Can I come from Tangier?

Yes, a couple of hours by coach or grand taxi — handy if you arrive in the north by ferry or flight.

What about a grand taxi?

Shared per-seat, leaving when full, faster and more flexible than the coach. Charter the whole car for about six seat fares.

How long should I stay?

Two nights fits best. The mountain journey each way takes real time, so treat it as a restful pause, not a day trip.

title: Arriving at Casablanca Airport: Your First Two Hours
content:
Casablanca's Mohammed V airport is where most flights from the US touch down, and for the classic first-timer loop it is usually a gateway rather than a destination — the goal is to move smoothly through it and on to Marrakech or Fez. The single fact that makes that easy is the train station directly beneath the terminal. Here is how the first two hours run, in order.

Through immigration

US citizens need no advance visa, so passport control is a stamp rather than an application: have your passport valid for the required period and know the address of your first night's accommodation, which the form may ask for. Lines vary with how many flights have landed together, so build a little patience into the plan. Check that your entry stamp is clear before you walk away, since a missing stamp becomes a question on the way out.

Cash before anything else

Because you cannot buy dirham before arriving, the airport ATM is the first real stop after immigration, and there are bank machines in the arrivals area. Withdraw enough for the first day or two, decline the "pay in dollars" conversion prompt in favour of dirham, and skip the exchange counter unless your card fails. With cash in hand and your phone connected, the rest of the arrival is simple logistics.

Connect and confirm

If you have not already, this is the moment to switch on your eSIM or buy a local SIM, then message your onward accommodation so they know you have landed. A connected phone with a map and your booking details turns the next steps from guesswork into a short checklist. It is the small piece of preparation that removes most first-hour friction.

The train under the terminal

The key to Casablanca airport is the ONCF train station directly beneath it, from which trains run to Casa Voyageurs — the main station — and onward across the network. This is why Casablanca works as an entry point even when the city is not your destination: you can land and be on a train toward Marrakech or Fez without setting foot in Casablanca proper. Check the departure board and buy your ticket at the counter or machine.

Onward to Marrakech or Fez

For Marrakech, you typically take the airport train to Casa Voyageurs and change to a Marrakech service; for Fez, a similar connection heads north and east. First class buys a reserved seat for a small premium, worth it with luggage after a long flight. The whole move — land, cash, train — can be done in well under two hours when flights and schedules cooperate.

If you're staying in Casablanca first

Some travellers spend a first night in Casablanca to break the journey or see the Hassan II Mosque, and that is a reasonable soft landing after a transatlantic flight. A petit taxi or the train reaches the city centre, and a night's rest before the onward leg suits anyone badly jet-lagged. For the classic loop, though, most push straight on while the momentum of arrival carries them.

Timing your connection

How much buffer to leave depends on your energy and your onward booking: trains from the airport station run regularly, so a missed connection rarely costs more than the wait for the next, but after a transatlantic flight a little slack is kindness to yourself. If you have booked a specific onward train, allow time for immigration lines and the walk down to the platform. If you have not, buying on arrival is straightforward outside peak crush.

Late-night landings

Flights from the US often land in the evening, and a late arrival changes the calculus: onward trains thin out at night, so an airport-area hotel or a first night in Casablanca can beat arriving in Marrakech in the small hours. Weigh the momentum of pushing on against the comfort of a bed nearby. Neither is wrong; it depends on the hour and how you travel tired.

The calm-arrival checklist

The whole first two hours reduce to a short sequence: clear immigration, withdraw dirham and decline the dollar conversion, connect your phone and message your accommodation, then take the train beneath the terminal onward. Done in that order, nothing catches you out, and you reach your real first destination with cash, a working phone, and a seat booked rather than a scramble at the rank.

The arrival hour is where the trip's habits are set: cash before you commit to any fare, the conversion prompt declined, the onward leg planned. How arrival, money and the first move fit together is worked out in the complete Morocco trip guide.

For getting dirham on landing, see our money-on-arrival guide; for the rail network onward, the trains guide covers routes and classes.

Casablanca airport arrival: FAQ

Is there a train at Casablanca airport?

Yes — an ONCF station directly beneath the terminal, with trains to Casa Voyageurs and onward across the network. It's the key to a smooth arrival.

Do I need a visa to enter?

No advance visa for US citizens. Passport control is a stamp — have your passport valid and your first address ready.

Where do I get dirham?

At a bank ATM in the arrivals area, right after immigration. Decline the "pay in dollars" prompt and choose dirham.

Can I go straight to Marrakech or Fez?

Yes. Take the airport train to Casa Voyageurs and connect onward. The whole move can take under two hours.

Should I stay a night in Casablanca?

Optional. It breaks the journey and allows a visit to the Hassan II Mosque, but most loop travellers push straight on.

title: Getting from Marrakech to Fez: Every Option
content:
Marrakech and Fez are the two anchors of a classic Morocco loop, and getting between them is one of the trip's defining logistical choices — not because it is hard, but because the option you pick reshapes the itinerary. You can take the direct train, a coach, a private driver, or fold the journey into a multi-day desert tour that turns the transfer into the highlight of the trip. Here is every option and when each makes sense.

The train: the standard choice

The ONCF train is the default way between Marrakech and Fez, a comfortable ride of roughly seven to eight hours, usually with a change at Casablanca, and it is the option most independent first-timers take. First class buys a reserved seat for a small premium — worth it on a journey this length, especially with luggage. It is calm, reliable and lets you read or watch the country pass, and it drops you in the centre of each city.

Why the train usually wins

For a straightforward city-to-city transfer, the train beats the alternatives on comfort and simplicity: no driving, no negotiation, a fixed schedule and a seat you can book. Booking a day ahead in high season secures first class. Unless you specifically want the desert in between or door-to-door service, the train is the sensible default, and the change at Casablanca is simple rather than a hassle.

The coach

A CTM coach runs the route too, comparable in time to the train and slightly cheaper, and it is a fine alternative if the train schedule does not suit or seats are sold out. It is comfortable and air-conditioned, though it lacks the train's room to move on a long journey. For most travellers the train edges it, but the coach is a solid backup and occasionally the better fit for timing.

The private driver

Hiring a private driver for the Marrakech-to-Fez run costs considerably more but buys door-to-door service and the freedom to stop along the way, and it makes most sense if you want to see sights between the cities rather than travel directly. A driver can route you past Beni Mellal or through scenery a train skips, turning the transfer into a touring day. For a family or a group, the cost per head narrows and the convenience can justify it.

Flying between them

There are also domestic flights on some city pairs, though for Marrakech to Fez the short flight time is usually outweighed by the airport rigmarole at both ends, and the train often wins door to door once you count check-in and transfers. Flying makes more sense for longer hops — reaching the far south or the coast — than for a route the train covers comfortably in an afternoon. For most first-timers, the direct train remains the better use of the day.

The desert tour route

The most rewarding option for many is not a direct transfer at all: a multi-day desert tour that starts in Marrakech and ends in Fez, crossing the High Atlas, Aït Benhaddou, the Dades Valley and the dunes of Merzouga on the way. This turns the journey between the cities into the centerpiece of the whole trip, and it neatly solves the transfer by making it the Sahara leg. If the desert is on your list, ending it in Fez is the elegant way to sequence a loop.

One-way tours solve the logistics

Because these tours run one-way, Marrakech to Fez, they save you doubling back over the long southern drive, and they fold the transport, the guide and the desert night into a single booking. It is the reason so many first-timer loops put the desert in the middle: you are travelling between the cities anyway, so you might as well do it through the Sahara. Confirm the tour ends in Fez when you book.

Whether the Marrakech-Fez leg is a train ride or the desert centerpiece is the single choice that most shapes a first loop's order and pace. How that decision ripples through the trip is worked out in the complete Morocco trip guide.

For the desert version, see our Sahara tours guide; for the rail option, the trains guide covers routes and classes.

Marrakech to Fez: FAQ

What's the best way from Marrakech to Fez?

The train for a direct transfer — about seven to eight hours, usually via Casablanca, comfortable and reliable. First class is worth it.

How long does the train take?

Roughly seven to eight hours with a change at Casablanca. Book first class a day ahead in high season for a reserved seat.

Is a private driver worth it?

If you want to stop at sights along the way or need door-to-door service, yes. It costs more but turns the transfer into a touring day.

Can I see the desert on the way?

Yes — a multi-day one-way desert tour from Marrakech to Fez crosses the Atlas and the dunes, turning the transfer into the trip's highlight.

Coach or train?

Similar time, coach slightly cheaper. The train edges it for comfort and room, but the coach is a solid backup.
